Md. Abdur Rahman Sikder --------- Petitioner
Vs.
Nur Mohammad Khan and others --------- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
2. The relevant facts are that the present petitioners as First party filed a petition on 30.1.04 under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure against the opposite parties nos.1 and 2 and 4-33 for drawing up a proceeding in respect of the disputed land measuring of 13.72 acres and to restrain members of the 2nd party from disturbing their possession. Prior to that, the 2nd  party as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit no. 30 of 94 (previous. number being Title Suit no. 20/92 Borguna, and 121/55, Barisal), in the Court of Joint District Judge, for establishment of title, confirmation of possession and also for partition; and a preliminary decree was passed in that suit giving saham of 6.80 acres to the plaintiffs —2nd parties and 11.10 acres to some of the defendants of that suit on 8.7.03. The land of the proceeding under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure also falls within the said decretal land. The First party petitioners preferred Title Appeal No. 63 of 2003 against the said decree before the District Judge, Borguna and operation of the judgment and decree was stayed on 7.8.03. Since the 2nd parties have threatened first party and tried to reap away the paddy from the disputed land by force thereby causing apprehension of breach of peace, the first party had to initiate the proceeding under sections 144/145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure during pendency of the Title Appeal no. 63 of 03. On the basis of a police report about the allegation of having apprehension of breach of peace, the Magistrate had drawn up the proceeding under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure on 24.12.03 restraining both the parties from entering into the case land. He also appointed Officer-in-Charge of the Police Station, Borguna, as Receiver of the disputed land by the same order. 

 3. Being aggrieved by the said order, the 2nd party nos. 1 and 24 preferred the Criminal Revision no.26 of 2004 before the Sessions Judge, Borguna, who was pleased to allow the revision case and thereby dropped the proceeding on setting aside the order of the Magistrate by the impugned judgment and order dated 15.9.04. Against the said judgment and order, the first party to the proceeding preferred the present application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure and obtained the Rule and stay order on 5.10.04. Soon after the opposite parties entered appearance and submitted an application to vacate the stay order the said application was previously disposed of their Lordships Mr. Justice S.K. Sinha and Mr Justice Shahidul Islam vide order dated 5.12.04 vacating the stay order, but on 12.12. 04, the unsigned order was recalled as the Court had no jurisdiction to deal with the matter at the relevant time. Thereafter the learned Hon'ble Chief Justice has sent the application for vacating the stay order to this Bench vide order dated 13.12.04. Since this Bench has constitution to make disposal of the original Criminal Misc. Case under section 561A. On the joint submission of the learned Advocates, we heard the matter without dealing with the application of vacating the stay order separately. 

 4. Mr. Md. Mojibur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the First party-petitioners, submits that the learned Sessions Judge has fallen in error of law in taking the view that the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to draw up a proceeding under section 145 Cr.P.C. when a decree of the Civil Court on the same subject matter had already been passed. Because; he submits, the preliminary decree of the Civil court was stayed by the Appellate Court in connection with the Title Appeal no. 63 of 2003 when the proceeding was drawn up by the Magistrate. According to his submissions the Suit was pending before appellate Court at that time, and mere pendency of the suit or appeal without having any order regulating possession of the disputed land does not create any bar to initiate proceeding under section 145 Cr.P.C., if the magistrate is satisfied that there is immediate apprehension of breach of peace over possession of the disputed land. In support of his contention, the learned Advocate cited the case decisions reported in 49 DLR 484, 45 DLR(AD) 31 and 35 DLR 180. With reference to those cases, the learned Advocate submits that the learned Sessions Judge has failed to consider that there was no enforce-able decree of the Civil Court in the eye of law at that time as the decree was stayed by the Appellate Court; and that the preliminary decree under challenge before the higher Court has not yet been made final regulating possession of the parties and as such the jurisdiction of the Magistrate in drawing up the proceeding under section 145 Cr.P.C. and passing an order of attachment thereunder was not ousted. The learned Advocate further submits that there was no interlocutory order of the Civil Court regulating possession of the parties at the relevant time and as such the impugned judgment setting aside the orders of the Magistrate is nothing but misconception of law and sheer abuse of the process of law, and as such, he submits that the impugned judgment is liable to be quashed. 

 5. Mr. S. M. Rezaul Karim, the learned Advocate for the 2nd party-opposite party nos.1 and 24, in reply, submits that on the application of 2nd party —plaintiffs for temporary injunction in Title Suit no. 30 of 1994, the learned Joint District Judge passed an order directing both the parties to maintain status-quo in respect possession vide order no. 29 dated 1.12.92, and on the basis of such order, plaintiffs- 2nd party was able to maintain their possession in the disputed land and no problem arose in between the parties so long and ultimately the decree was passed finding the plaintiff —opposite parties in possession of their claimed land (6.80 acre). Therefore, the Civil Court was very much in the seisin of the subject matter on the question of title and possession. But the learned Magistrate appears to have assumed jurisdiction under section 145 Cr.P.C. inspite of having knowledge that the Civil Court had already passed a decree involving the question of possession and he also appointed a Receiver to dislodge possession of the parties which is not at all permissible in law. He submits that in a proceeding under section 145 of the Code, the Magistrate is required to determine possession of the parties in the absence of decision of the Civil Court and if necessary, keep the disputed property under attachment and then ask the parties to take shelter before the Civil Court for determination of title and possession. But when the parties already took shelter in the Civil Court long before and dispute was pending in appeal, the order of the Magistrate was malafide and it amounts to abuse of the process of the Court and as such the learned Sessions Judge has decided the legal question in right direction which does not call for interference. 

 7. On perusal of these case decisions, it is clear that the settled law on the subject is that when the Civil Court is already seized with the subject matter in dispute and has passed any order regulating possession or passed a decree for possession, the jurisdiction of the Magistrate to act under section 145 Cr.P.C. is ousted. In such case, if any law and order situation arises involving the disputed landed property, the only course open to the Magistrate is to take action under section 107/117 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to prevent apprehended breach of peace. In the case of Nader Ali SK. Vs. The State reported in 35 DLR-180, it was held that mere pendency of a Civil Suit is no bar to the institution of a proceeding under section 145 Cr.P.C., if the Magistrate is satisfied that there is an immediate apprehension of breach peace over the possession in the disputed land. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has relied on the said decision with the contention that the appeal being continuation of the original suit, is necessarily a pending case and as such jurisdiction of the Magistrate was not ousted in dealing with the proceeding. 

 8. In the instance case, the 2nd party opposite parties being plaintiffs instituted Title Suit no. 30 of 94 (renumbered from original Title Suit no. 121 of 55 of Barisal, and 20 of 1992 of Borguna) against the First party petitioners and others for establishment of title, confirmation of possession and also for partition of their share to the existent of 6 .80 acres out of the total 22.56 acres of land. It is admitted that the 2nd party-plaintiffs had homestead within the said share of land claimed by them in the suit. Annexure-1 to the supplementary affidavit of the opposite parties shows that on 1.12.92, the plaintiffs 2nd party submitted an application under order 39 Rule 1 C.P.C. for temporary injunction in Title Suit no. 30 of 94 against the defendants-first party to restrain them from interfering with their possession in the said land measuring 6.80 acres. On that date, the learned Subordinate Judge, First Court, Borguna vide order no. 29 dated 1.12.92 directed both the parties to maintain status-quo in respect of their possession in the case land. It appears that the said order of the Civil Court regulating possession in the land had served the purpose of the parties for a long time and the suit was ultimately decreed on contest on 8.7.03. It transpires from the judgment passed in Title Suit no. 30 of 94 that the Civil Court allotted 6.80 acres of land to the Saham of the 2nd party-plaintiffs on being satisfied that they have right, title and possession therein. Issue no. 4 of the suit relates to the disputed question of right, title and possession of the parties. The learned Joint District Judge also granted saham to many of the defendants to the existent 11.10 acres for effecting partition. The petitioners first party has not taken any ground in the application under section 561-A of the Code of Criminal procedure to the effect that the decretal land does not include the lands of the proceeding drawn up under section 145 Cr.P.C. Thus it is clear from the documents, on record that the 2nd party opposite parties got decree from the competent Civil Court in respect of the same subject matter of the.145 proceeding even after adjudication of title and possession of the same parties in the disputed land. It appears further that during long pendency of the title suit, there was an interlocutory order regulating possession of the parties in the disputed land. 

 9. After filing of Title Appeal no. 63 of 2003, the appellants (first party) submitted an application for staying operation of the judgment and decree appealed against which was granted by the learned District Judge, Borguna on 7.8.2003 vide Annexure-E. Subsequently, on 13.11.03, the appellants- first party filed an application before the Magistrate, Borguna under section 144/145 Cr.P.C. for initiating a proceeding against the said decree holder 2nd party; and the Magistrate, on obtaining a police report dated 4.12.03 (Annexure-B), had passed the disputed order dated 24.12.03 drawing up a proceeding and appointed a Receiver by the same order. He also restrained both the parties from entering in the case land which includes the decretal land of the other side. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has strenuously argued that since the decree of the trial Court was stayed by the Appellate Court, the appeal, being a continuation of the original suit, was nothing but a pending suit and there having no injunction order of the Civil Court regulating possession of the parties at the relevant time, the Magistrate acted properly in accordance with provisions of section 145 Cr.P.C. But such type interpretation, if considered acceptable, will create a far reaching effect and a party, already involved in the Civil Case claiming title and possession, shall get scope to go to the criminal Court to take undue advantage against the rival party and dislodge existing possession through appointment of Receiver. Section 145 Cr.P.C. is intended only to provide a quick temporary remedy for prevention of breach of peace arising out of claim and counter claim of possessory right in the immoveable property. The object of the section 145 is to enable the Magistrate intervene and pass a temporary order regulating possession - in the disputed land until the actual right of one party is fully determined by the competent Civil Court. So in the absence of such a decision or decree of the Civil Court, the Magistrate can proceed under this section to determine disputed question of possession. But when a decision has already been arrived at by the competent Civil Court relating ownership and possession, it should be respected by the Magistrate. There should not be any scope to unsettle the matter of possession by giving appointment of a Receiver and dispossess one party to the disadvantage of another and pave the way to dispossess any party as has been done in the present case. It is true that the decree of the Civil Court .was under challenge before the Appellate Court and it is yet to be made final keeping operation of the decree stayed till disposal of the appeal, so that the decree can not be put to execution till it reaches its finality. But such stay order does not mean that any party to the suit or appeal will take advantage of the situation and avail of the forum of the Magistrate Court in order unsettle the existing decision of the Civil Court regarding possession of the parties through appointment of a Receiver. Since the Appellate Court is already in the seisin of the matter including adjudication of possessory right of the parties over it, it has got exclusive authority to decide whether the verdict of the trial Court is correct or not. Till such final decision, change of possession in the subject matter, as found by the trial Court, is not expected to be interfered with by the Magistrate under section 145 Cr.P.C. The aggrieved party is, however, be liberty to seek restraining order before the Appellate Court during pendency of the Appeal, if so necessary. Since there is pending appeal over the dispute, after having a decree of the trial Court regulating the questions of right, title and possession and there was order of status-quo during long pendency of the suit from 1.12.1992 to 8.7. 2003, we hold the view that the Magistrate having no jurisdiction had illegally entertained the proceeding under section 145 Cr.P.C. and appointed a Receiver having full knowledge about the decree of the Civil Court. The facts and circumstances of the present case, if considered properly, definitely come within the ambit of the broad principles enunciated in the reported decisions already cited above wherein it is held that when the Civil Court is already seized with the question of regulating possession of the land between the same parties, the jurisdiction of the Magistrate under section 145 Cr.P.C. is ousted. In the case of Abul Basher and another = vs = Hasanuddin Ahmed and others reported in 51 DLR(AD) –14, their Lordships held-

Md. Mizanur Rahman Bhuiyan, J: This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 3.1.1993 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Patuakhali, in Title Suit No. 299 of 1990 should not be set aside or such other or further order or orders passed as to this court may deem fit and proper. 

 2. The fact relevant for disposal of the rule, in short, is that the opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 299 of 1990 in the Court of the learned Assistant Judge, Patuakhali for declaration that the ex-parte decree on 21-1-90 in favour of defendant-petitioner in Title Suit No. 186 of 1989 in 'Ka' schedule of land in place of `Kha' schedule is illegal, collusive, fraudulent and liable to be set aside. The defendant No. 1 the petitioner, contested the suit by filing written statements denying all the material allegations made in the plaint. On 27.7.1992 the suit was posted for hearing and a petition for time on behalf of the plaintiff-opposite party on that date was refused by the learned Assistant Judge who had directed the parties to be ready for hearing of the case but the plaintiff was absent when the said case was called on for hearing and that the learned Assistant Judge, Patuakhali having not found the plaintiff-opposite party had dismissed the Title Suit No. 299 of 1990. Thereafter on the same day the said opposite party had filed a petition under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the earlier order of the learned Assistant Judge and that the learned Assistant Judge had fixed 3.9.1992 for hearing the said petition. On 2.9.1992 the defendant-petitioner had filed written objection against the said prayer of the plaintiff-opposite party under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure after serving a copy to the plaintiff-opposite party alleging that there is specific remedy of the plaintiff-opposite party against the order of the learned Assistant Judge dismissing the suit for default on 27.7.92 and as such the petition for setting aside the aforesaid order dated 27.7.92 under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure is not maintainable in law which is liable to be rejected. On 3.1.93 the learned Assistant Judge after hearing the parties had allowed the prayer of the plaintiff-opposite party under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and passed the order for restoration of the Original Title Suit No. 299 of 1990 after setting aside his earlier order of dismissal of the suit for default dated 27.7.1992.
