parties:
Aftabuddin Ahmed ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Commerce, Special Property Cell and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
3. The land of plot 6436 measuring .0956 acres recorded in khatian No. 3691 as cultivable vacant land within Sylhet Municipality. Kalighat, was acquired by purchase in 1949 (1356 BS) by one Duraram Upadhyaya, S/o. Late Thoparam Upadhyaya from the original owner Rakesh Chandra Kar and others. During the last Settlement Survey the said land was wrongly recorded in the names of the heirs of original owners and on a petition of objection by the said Duraram Upadhyaya, the CO (Rev) Sadar Sylhet by order dated 15.12.62 allowed the objection and directed correction of the record of rights in the names of the Duraram, as purchaser in possession without document. Thereafter in respect of the lands Duraram obtained a Registered kobala dated 25.4.63 executed and registered by Rakhal Kanti Kar and Jahar Kanti Kar, sons of late Rakesh Chandra Kar, This said Duraram Upadhyaya was in exclusive ownership and possession of the said plot of land for long over the period of limitation. Then he transferred the land to the petitioner for a consideration of Taka 3000.00 by a registered kabala dated 4.8.72. The kabala was executed and registered in pursuance of a Deed of Agreement for sale by Duraram earlier made on 5.1.68. Thereafter the petitioner mutated his name in the khatian vide order dated 19.8.72 passed by CO (Rev). Kotwali, Sylhet and he was continuing to be in possession thereof as exclusive owner of the land on payment of rents to the Government and Taxes to the Municipality. He also raised Bank Loan for his business by mortgaging the property within the knowledge of the Additional Deputy Commissioner Sylhet who was also the Chairman of the Loan Sanctioning Board. 

 6. The petitioner's brother (added respondent No.4) turned inimical to the petitioner and he was trying to take lease of the property. So the petitioner had to file Title Suit No. 81 of 1972 in the Second Court as Subordinate Judge, Sylhet for declaration of Title and confirmation of possession with further declaration that it was not an enemy or abandoned property. He also prayed for temporary injunction restraining the Government and other defendants from disturbing his peaceful possession. The suit was, however, dismissed for default on 19.8.75 and the petitioner brought the Misc. Case No. 37 of 76 for its restoration. But this case also was dismissed on 30.10.78. The petitioner then applied to the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms for release of the property from the list of vested properties and later he filed petition before the Secretary, Ministry of Commerce and Foreign Trade, Government of Bangladesh, who was pleased to stay all actions of proposed lease by the order dated 7.8.78. But the Deputy Commissioner, Sylhet (respondent No. 2) took forcible possession of the petitioners' property on 15.11.78. Then the petitioner filed an application before the Ministry of Commerce and Foreign Trade but without any effect. Against this forcible possession of the property on 15.11.78 by the order of respondent No. 2 dated 14.11.78 the petitioner moved this court in writ petition No. 14 of 1979. Their Lordships Mr. Justice Chowdhury ATM Masud and Mr. Justice MH Rahman by judgment and order dated 18.7.80 were pleased to direct restoration of the properties to the petitioner, with an observation that, "this however will not stand in the way of the Respondents to take any legal action in the matter in accordance with law" In pursuance of this decision, the property was restored to the petitioner by an order of the ADC Sylhet under Memo No. SA/lI-I/ P-13/78/10628(4) dated 11.12.80. Thereafter, the petitioner was served with the impugned notice dated 3.10.81 by the Deputy Commissioner, Respondent No. 2 asking him to show cause within 7(seven) days of receipt of the notice as to why he will not be evicted being an unauthorised occupant in the said property on the ground that no right or title of the petitioner over the property was declared in the aforesaid Writ Petition No. 14 of 1979 (Annexure E). 

 7. The petitioner had shown cause by filing a petition of objection on 12.10.61 to the Deputy Commissioner, Sylhet. He pleaded that the disputed land in plot No. 6436 of Mouza Sylhet Municipality was a fallow land and not connected with or a part of "Tobacco Mollasses and Khamfia shop" of Messrs Chandmal, Surajmal Bantia, Kalighat, Sylhet" with whom Duraram Upadhyaya had no connection or concern. The 'corrigendum' issued in Gazette Notification dated 6.5.67 did not vest the property of the petitioner in the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property for Sylhet and that the petitioner was in possession of the property on the basis of valid title by dint, amongst other things, of a registered kabala dated 4.8.72. 

 "Perused the records The earlier order stands in view of the fact that the Hon'ble High Court has not given any adjudication regarding right and title of the property. It is still considered to be a vested property and therefore please take action accordingly." The petitioner expressed his grievance that he was not granted certified copy of the aforesaid order passed by the respondent No. 2. 

 9. The petitioner has obtained this Rule mainly on the grounds that the impugned Gazette notifications do not attract the disputed properties which belonged to the petitioner and secondly that in the circumstances of the case, if the Government wanted to claim title in the property in question it could only do so by way of appropriate suit for declaration of title and cancellation of the petitioner's registered kabala and other deeds in view of decision of the Appellate Division, setting down principles governing cases of this nature. 

 11. The Rule was opposed by the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 and also by the added respondent No. 4 who file affidavits in opposition. The respondent Nos. 1 and 2 and the added respondent No. 4 had controverted the material allegations. They, in substance, contended that the plot No. 6436 was not a cultivable land but a place of the shopping centre in the best commercial area within Sylhet Municipality. Rakesh Chandra Kar and others abandoned the land, left for India long before the final publication of the last Khatian Duraram Upadhyaya had no right, title or interest in the property. He got his name recorded in respect of the property through a got up objection case by practising fraud and influencing the settlement staff with a view to grabbing the property. Later on 25.4.63 he falsely created a kabala in his favour and recorded his name in the khatian. The kabala dated 4.8.72 by Duraram in favour of the petitioner was fraudulent and forged. The alleged agreement in pursuance of which the kabala was executed was also false. The order dated 19.8.72 relating to recording of the petitioner's name in the khatian was on the basis of his fraudulent agreement and sale deeds respectively dated 5.1.68 and 4.8.72, when Duraram was not residing in this country. He left for India during Indo-Pak war in 1965. Thus the petitioner had no right, title and interest in the property by virtue of his payment of Municipal or any other taxes, nor could he legally obtain any loan by mortgage of the land; nor did he ever file any application for loan to the officer concerned, i.e. the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue). It was further contended by the respondents that the land in question was Enemy Property. The petitioner had taken lease of the land in the name of his brother Faizuddin Ahmed but at the instigation of the petitioner, his brother instead of renewing the lease, filed Title Suit Nos. 334 of i967 and 163 of 1971 in the Courts of 2nd Sub-Judge and 1st Munsif respectively without any success, the petitioner claimed his own title in the land and filed Title Suit No. 81 of 1972 in the Court of 2nd Sub-Judge, Sylhet. His claim was false. So he allowed the suit to be dismissed. Then he filed Misc. Appeal No. 37 of 1975 in the Court of District Judge, Sylhet for setting aside the order of dismissal and restoration of the case but that Misc. Appeal was also dismissed on contest. Then the petitioner got Title Suit No. 525 of 1976 of the Court of 2nd Sub-Judge by one Goura Chandra Das showing him as tenant under him. This suit was also dismissed. The respondents further contended that the petitioner had no title whatsoever in the land and the papers in support of the claim filed by the petitioner were fabricated. The respondents contended that the disputed property was declared as Enemy Property by Notification of January 7, 1966 as corrected by one dated 6.5.67. The plot Nos. 6436 and 6435 were contiguous plots and Messers Chandmahal Surjamal Bantia was a well-known business house that had several shops upon the same. When the owners of the said business house had left for India in September, 1965, the property came under the control and management of the authority concerned as vested property and it was taken lease of as such in the name of the petitioner's brother Faizuddin Ahmed (added respondent No. 4). It has been contended by the respondents that the petitioner was trespasser and he was asked to vacate the land. After he vacated the land possession was taken over by the respondent Nos. 1 and 2. But in obedience to Writ Petition No. 14/79 the respondents restored possession to the petitioner and served him with a legal notice under section 5 of the Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) Administration and Disposal Order, 1966. 

 13. The main grounds urged by Mr. Azizur Rahman Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, are that the concerned Gazette Notifications do not attract the disputed properties and therefore, the disputed properties have never been treated as Enemy Property or vested properties. Again, when the petitioner has been in possession of the disputed property on the basis of title, the respondents are not entitled to evict the petitioner in pursuance of the impugned notice under section 5 of the Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) Administration and Disposal Order 1966 (Annexure G) without enforcing the claim of the respondents in a proper forum and the respondents cannot evict the petitioner summarily without having recourse to the civil Court for decision as to the title of the petitioner. 

 14. Annexure A to the petition is the Gazette Notification No. Sec-140/65/8 EPS dated January 7, 1966 and Annexure B is its Corrigendum Sec-III/IV-9/67/271 EPC dated 6th May, 1967. Gazette Notification No Sec-140/63/8 EPS 7th January, 1966 gives a schedule of properties which have been directed by the Government to be listed as Vested Properties of the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property Sylhet District, Serial No. 16 of the schedule to the notification is Tobacco, Molasses and khamfia shop of Messers Chandmal Surajmal Bantia Kalighat, Sylhet. The Corrigendum dated 6th May, 1967 says that the following may be read in place of the existing one. No. 16 "Messers Chandmal Surajmal Bantia including Dhura Ram Upadhyay, son of Lunaram Upadhyay, Kalighat, Sylhet", The stand of the respondents is that by means of this Corrigendum, the Tobacco, Molasses and Khamfia shop of Messers Chandmal Surajmal Bantia, Kalighat, Sylhet was also considered to be inclusive of the property of Dhura Ram. It was to be seen that neither in original notification nor in Corrigendum, the plot number or area of the property was given. Now the petitioner has appended Annexures C and D to the petition. Annexure C shows that the plot No. 6435 stood recorded in the name of Sushil Chandra Chowdhury and others and the property was described as 'Gudam Ghar' Annexure D, on the other hand, shows that Dag No. 6436 was vacant property of Sushil Chandra Chowdhury and others but possession was of Dhura Ram Upadhyay, son of Lunaram Upadhyaya, the vendor of the petitioner who was in possession of this plot No. 6436 with effect from 1356 BS and the petitioner Aftabuddin Ahmed had mutated his name in respect of this khatian by order dated 22.4.77. These two Annexures show that the plot Nos. 6435 and 6436 were two distinct lands both originally belonging to Shushil Chandra Chowdhury, The affidavit-in-opposition shows that these two plots are adjacent. Although these two plots are adjacent, they constitute two different khatians namely khatian No. 3431 and khatian No. 3691. The petitioner's case is that the Tobacco, Molasses and Khamfia shop of Messrs Chandmal Surajmal Bantia, Kalighat, Sylhet is situated upon dag No. 6435 and not upon dag No. 6436. Plot No. 6436 was originally the property of Sushil Chandra Chowdhury and from him Duraram Upadhayay purchased the land and he in his turn sold it to the petitioner Aftabuddin Ahmed in the year 1972. Now it is easy to see that the Gazette Notification Annexure A and its Corrigendum Annexure B are vague and they do not show whether the dag No. 6435 or 6436 or both of them were included in the Gazette Notification and in the Corrigendum. Therefore we find sound basis for the argument of the petitioner that his property was not as a matter of fact published in the Gazette as enemy property. 

 15. Secondly the petitioner has produced the certified copy of the kabala executed by Duraram Updhyaya on 4.8.72. The petitioner, as it appears from the Annexure L to the petitioner's affidavit- in-reply, had submitted certified copy of this document also before the respondent No. 2 in support of his objection filed on 3.10.81. It is at serial No. 8 of the Annexure. The petitioner has stated in his writ petition that he had submitted the original of this kabala to the Pubali Bank for obtaining loan for making construction upon the land of dag No. 6436. The petitioner has filed a certificate from the Ministry to the effect that the petitioner Mr. Aftabuddin Ahmed, Proprietor M/S Kalighat Flour Mills Kalighat, Sylhet has been enjoying a cash credit facility under BSCIC Loan from that Branch against which he offered certain documents of landed property. Serial No. I of these documents is Original Title deed comprising 9 decimal land under dag No. 6436, khatian No. 1809, JL No. 91 Mouza-Sylhet Municipality owned by Mr. Aftabuddin Ahmed, son of late Usman Ali of Kalighat, Sylhet, This serial No. 1 obviously refers to the original of the kabala furnished before this Court executed by Duraram Upadhyaya. The petitioner has also appended to this affidavit-in-reply Annexures I, J, and K which prima facie bear out that the petitioner had established Flour Mills upon the land in plot 6436. 

 16. The above documents and the averments supported by affidavit by the petitioner clearly show that the petitioner has a prima facie title. It appears that the petitioner was once dispossessed from the disputed land by the respondent No. 2 without any notice under section 4 of the Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) Administration and Disposal Order, 1966 and the petitioner had brought an application under Article 102 of the Constitution being Writ Petition No. 14 of 1979 before this court and their Lordships Mr. Justice Chowdhury ATM Masud and Mr. Justice MH Rahman found fault with the eviction, in that no notice was served upon the petitioner prior to the eviction. Their Lordships stated all the facts of the case but refrained from giving any decision as to the title of the petitioner or of the respondents. Their Lordships observed. 

 "It has been consistently held, in our opinion rightly held in these cases, the vesting of property in the Custodian of Enemy Property did not transgress upon the title of the real owner and that nobody in possession of such property in exercise of a right, however imperfect or limited it may be, can be said to be in unlawful possession within the meaning of paragraph 5 of the Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) Administration and Disposal Order, 1966," It was correctly observed by Chief Justice Siddiky (Abdul Hakim, J agreeing), who was incidentally a party to the judgment under appeal, on construing the provision of Rule 192 of the Defence of Pakistan Rules, in the case of Ananda Mohan Kundu and others Vs. Province of East Pakistan 20 DLR 976, 980 "If after vesting of the enemy property in the Custodian, it is found on enquiry that a person who is holding some sort of document of title, though imperfect, from the real owner of the property who happended to be the enemy, then if the occupier is a citizen of Pakistan he cannot be Custed from the property because of mere vesting order of the Government. In paragraph 37, their Lordships observed: 

 "Where circumstances of a case establish that a person in possession of a property treated as enemy property has set up and proved a prima facie title to the same, it amounts to this that the question that his possession of the property was illegal was in issue and therefore such possession cannot be treated illegal without a decision of this question in a properly constituted suit." 

 The authority in the Government could not question and annul the validity of such title by an executive order. If the Government wanted to claim the title in such property it could only do so by way of an appropriate suit for declaration of title and cancellation of the registered kabala as such. Again in the case of Abul Khair Miah being dead his heirs Abul Kashem and others Vs. Bangladesh and others reported in 29 DLR (AD) 29 their Lordships of the Appellate Division observed: 

 The aforesaid decisions lay down the principles that whenever an individual is in possession of a property on the basis of some sort of title deed either by way of purchase or unauthorised from the original owner said to be the enemy, the authority first of all has to establish that title in favour of the individual was invalid, void or fraudulent and this can be done at the instance of the authority by a properly constituted suit before the civil Court. In the instant case we find that the petitioner has furnished sufficient documents to establish this prima facie title and even if his title is invalid or bad in law it would be a matter to be decided by the civil Court. 

 It is for the authority to go to the civil Court and to get decision as to title and find whether they are allowed to evict the petitioner by means of notice under section 5 of the Enemy Property (Lands and Buildings) Administration and Disposal Order, 1966. 

 20. A question arose whether the dismissal for default of Title Suit No. 31 of 1972 would be a bar to the present writ application. We have given our consideration to the aspect of the case as well. The suit appears to have been dismissed for default under Order 9 rule 9. The petitioner filed an application for setting aside the dismissal order and to restore it to its original file and number in accordance with Order 9 rule 9 CPC. The Misc. Case was also dismissed on contest. Order 9 rule 9 precludes the plaintiff from bringing a fresh suit. But if a suit is dismissed for default in presence of defendant or defendants, the only remedy is under Order 9 rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure Order 9 rule 9, therefore, does not preclude the writ application before this court.

parties:
Mahananda Mondal and others………………….Petitioner
VS
Surajit Mondal and others……………………..Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
3. Relevant facts for disposal of the Rule are that opposite parties as plaintiff filed the Title Suit No. 6 of 1995 in the Court of learned Assistant Judge, Mongla, Bagerhat for partition. The suit was dismissed on 5-11-1995. Against that judgment and decree the plaintiffs preferred an appeal being No. 54 of 1996 which was allowed ex-parte and the suit was sent back on remand. Thereafter/the suit was decreed ex-parte on 3-7-2006. Against that judgment and decree defendant No. 2 Dinomoni Mondal filed Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2011 under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex-parte decree. That Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 2011 was allowed on 23-3-2015 by the learned Assistant Judge, Mongla, Bagerhat. Against that judgment and order the plaintiffs filed revision before the learned District Judge, Bagerhat being Civil Revision No. 11 of 2015 which was allowed setting aside the judgment and order passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Mongla, Bagerhat. 

 5. Ms. Promila Biswas, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners submits that the summons of Title Suit No. 6 of 1995 was not served upon the defendant Dinomoni Mondal. The plaintiff of the suit obtained decree by practicing fraud upon the court by suppressing service of summons. 

 7. Ms. Purabi Saha, learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parties contended that summons notices of the original Title Suit No. 6 of 1995 were duly served upon the defendants. She also submits that after the death of her husband she used to live with Mohananda Mondal who was another defendant in Title Suit No. 6 of 1995. Moreover, Mohanonda Mondal filed another Title Suit No. 25 of 2009 about the disputed land and Dinomoni Mondal fully aware of the suit No. 6 of 1995. Under such circumstances the petitioner is not entitled to get relief as prayed for. 

 9. I have heard both the sides and gone through the materials on record meticulously. Whether summons was served upon the defendant Dinomoni Mondal or not it is the vital question in this case. As per provisions of the Evidence Act, burden lies upon the plaintiff to prove that summons was duly served upon the defendant Dinomoni Mondal. Regarding this matter, the plaintiffs examined two witnesses including the plaintiff No. 4 Pijus Mondal as OPW 1 and Process Server Piar Ali as OPW 2. OPW 1 Pijus Mondal stated in his examination in-chief that summons of original suit was duly served, but in his cross-examination he stated that Dinomoni Modnal came before the process server and in presence of him Piar Ali served summons to Dinomoni Mondal and she received summons putting her signature. But, he stated in his cross-examination that Dinomoni Mondal received the summons putting her finger impression which is contradictory to his earlier statement that she received summons putting her signature. Process server Piar Ali was examined as OPW 2 who deposed that in that suit he served notice only upon Dinomoni Mondal. Notice was marked as Exhibit 'ka' but in his cross-examination he stated that he has served summons upon the defendant No. 9 Nilima only and he did not serve any summons to anybody except Nilima. Admittedly there is no defendant namely Nilima in the original partition suit. Under such circumstances the learned Assistant Judge, Mongla, Bagerhat decided that notice was not duly served upon the defendant Dinomoni Mondal and accordingly, he allowed the Miscellaneous Case No. No. 4 of 2011 filed under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 10. From the judgment passed by the learned District Judge, Bagerhat it appears that he has set-aside the judgment and order passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Mongla, Bagerhat by a long judgment without giving reasonable grounds. He did not consider whether the process or summons was_ duly served upon the defendant No. 1 or not. The learned District Judge, Bagerhat decided that summons was duly served upon the defendant Dinomoni Mondal since after the demise of her husband she was residing in the house of Mohananda Mondal who was plaintiff No. 1 in the original suit for which summons to be considered as duly served under Order V, rule 15 of the Code of Civil Procedure. But there is no material on record from which it can be ascertained that the summons in the name of Dinomoni Mondal was received by Mohananda Mondal on behalf of Dinomoni Mondal and at the time of service of summons she was residing in the house of Mohananda Mondal. 

 11. The learned District Judge stated in his judgment that Nilima was not a defendant in the original suit and the process server OPW 2 Piar All wrongly said in his cross-examination that defendant No. 9 was Nilima and he served summons only in the name of Nilima. Whenever it came to the knowledge of the learned District Judge that Nilima was not a defendant and the process server stated in his cross-examination that he served summons only in the name of Nilima, then he should have taken decision that service of summons upon the defendant Dinomoni Mondal was not proved. Inspite of that he decided wrongly that summons was served duly upon Dinomoni Mondal. The learned District Judge did not consider that the OPW 1 Pijus Mondal did not state a single sentence in this chief that summons of the original suit was served upon the defendant Dinomoni Mondol. Even he did not consider that the OPW-1 in his cross made contradictory statements as to receiving of summons by the defendant Dinomoni Mondal since he firstly stated that Dinomoni Mondal received the summons putting her signature and later he stated that she put her finger impression at the time of receiving summons. 

 12. It is transpired from the materials on record that the opposite parties failed to prove that the summons of the original suit was duly served upon the defendant-petitioner Dinomoni Mondal. The learned Assistant Judge rightly decided that the summons upon the defendant Dinomoni Mondal was not duly served. 

 14. In the case of Regent Ken International Ltd. vs Amanat Shah Ship Breaking Industries Ltd. reported in 57 DLR 234 (para-7) their Lordships held that if a party satisfies a Court that summons was not duly served upon him, the Court is bound to set-aside the ex-parte decree. In such a case, question of knowledge is not at all relevant and ex-parte decree will be set-aside even if the defendant had knowledge of institution of the suit. In the facts of the instant case, it is proved that the petitioner Dinomoni Mondal was not served with notices of the original suit and that was the cause for her non appearance when the suit was called on for hearing. 

 15. In the light of above deliberation, it is decided that the learned District Judge, Bagerhat wrongly decided that summons was served duly upon the defendant Dinomoni Mondal and, as such, he committed an error of law resulting an error in his decision occasioning failure of justice. So, the learned Assistant Judge, Mongla, Bagerhat- rightly decided that the summons was not duly served upon the defendant Dinomoni Mondal and he rightly restored the original suit in its original file and number. In fact, the plaintiff-opposite parties obtained judgment and decree in the original suit fraudulently by suppressing summons. It is settle principle of law that fraud vitiates everything. So, the judgment and decree passed in the original suit is not sustainable. 

 20. The ex-parte decree passed in Title Suit No. 6 of 1995 is hereby set-aside. The trial court is hereby directed to dispose of the suit expeditiously without unnecessary delay.

parties:
Hamida Begum and others --------- Petitioners
Vs.
Fayez Ahmed Chowdhury being dead his legal heirs 1(i) Nazemuddin Chowdhury and others --------- Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
The case of the plaintiff, inter alia, is that the plaintiff was the owner of the land in schedule-I (hereinafter referred to as the suit land), defendant No. 1 is the distant relative of the plaintiff and defendant No. 2 is the husband of the defendant No. 1. In the 1st part of 1985, the defendant No. 2 told the plaintiff that he needs the suit land for extension of his dwelling house and proposed to exchange the same with the land of schedule II belonging to defendant No. 1. The plaintiff agreed and accordingly, on 13.03.1985 a deed of exchange was executed and registered between the plaintiff and the defendant No. 1 and the plaintiff delivered possession of the suit land to the defendant and it was agreed that the defendants would deliver possession and handover title deeds of the schedule-II land on 14.03.1985, but till now the defendant did not deliver possession to the plaintiff on different pleas. The plaintiff being an old man has been suffering from different types of ailment could not communicate with the defendant. Failure of the defendant to deliver the possession of the land of schedule-II created suspicion in the mind of the plaintiff regarding ownership of defendant No.1 in the suit land. On enquiry the plaintiff came to know that the defendant No. 1 has/had no title in the schedule-II land, but got the deed of exchange executed by false representation. On 20.12.1996, the plaintiff asked the defendant to deliver possession of the suit land but the defendant refused, hence, the plaintiff filed the present suit. 

 The land of schedule-II along with other lands originally belonged to Abdur Rashid Chowdhury who settled the same in favour of one Mahfuzur Rabbi by Patta dated 19.05.1936. Mahfuzur Rabbi died leaving Jamaluddin and others as his heirs, accordingly, B.S. khatian (the latest records of right) stands recorded in the name of Jamaluddin and others, who by two kabalas dated 08.11.1978 sold the same to the brother of defendant No. 1, Md. Shawkat Alam. Subsequently, Shawkat Alam sold 10 decimals of land to the defendant No. 1 by kabala dated 16.06.1984. Said land is situated near Chakaria College. The plaintiff was looking for a piece of land in the said area to construct a house in order to provide accommodation to his children and grand children who were studying in Chakaria College and having come to know that the land of schedule II belonged to the defendant No. 1, was considered by him suitable to construct house and proposed the defendant to sell the said land to the plaintiff. The defendant considering the balance of convenience and inconveniences agreed to transfer the said land (schedule-II) by way of exchange with the suit land, accordingly, the plaintiff and the defendant No. 1 without being influenced or misrepresented by anybody executed and registered the deed of exchange on 13.03.1985 and delivered possession of their respective land to each other. The defendant by consolidating the land with the non-suited land (earlier purchased from Mostaque Ahmed) constructed semi pucca house thereon and planted fruit bearing trees and has been living thereon beyond the statutory period of limitation on payment of rents to the Government and Municipal taxes. On the other hand the plaintiff also having got the land of schedule-II bounded the same by fence and has been possessing by growing fruit bearing trees thereon. Since, the price of the suit land increased the same fell into the greedy eyes of the relatives of the plaintiff who with a view to grab the suit land managed the plaintiff to file the suit. The suit is false and frivolous and gambling in litigation, as such, prayed for dismissal of the suit. 

 The learned trial court after hearing the parties, found, inter alia, that the suit is not barred by limitation, title and possession of the defendant No. 1 in respect of land of schedule-II has not been proved, consequently, she could not deliver possession to the plaintiff and accordingly, decreed the suit by judgment and decree dated 07.06.1998 declaring the Exchange deed No. 1756 dated 13.03.1985 voidable and cancelled and directed the defendants to surrender possession of the suit land to the plaintiff within 90 days. 

 Mr. Md. Nurul Amin, Senior Advocate with Mr. Sayed Misbahul Anwar, learned Advocates appearing for the petitioner at the very outset submit that the deed of exchange in question admittedly executed and registered on 13.03.1985 and the plaintiff claimed that the defendant No. 1 had to deliver possession of the property and handover all the title documents to him on the following day i.e. on 14.03.1985, but taking various pleas the defendants delayed delivery of possession and documents such statements amply proves that the plaintiff knowing fully well about title of the defendants in suit executed and registered the deed of exchange, exchanging the suit property with the defendant No. 1. He further argued that since there is no allegation of fraud and misrepresentation on the part of the defendant, the plaintiff ought to have filed the suit for cancellation of the deed within three years from 14.03.1985 as provided in Article 91 of the Limitation Act, but the suit was filed after near about 12 years beyond the prescribed period of limitation, as such, both the courts below fell in serious error in not finding that the suit is hopelessly barred by limitation. 

 He further submits that in the impugned deed of exchange no stipulation was provided for cancellation of the deed for any defect in title or any fault, but there was a stipulation that the plaintiff would be entitled to claim market value of the property with compensation from the defendants and in the event of refusal by the defendants to pay the same could have filed a suit for recovery of market value of the property with compensation, but the plaintiff filed the suit praying for cancellation of deed of exchange and recovery of possession which is absolutely beyond the terms and conditions of the deed of exchange and section 119 of the Transfer of Property Act. 

 He further argued that both the courts below utterly failed to find the stipulation contain in the deed of exchange and the observations of both the courts below in this regard is contrary to the provision of section 119 of the Transfer of Property Act. It is also argued that the defendant No. 1 by producing chain of documents and adducing evidences proved her title in the schedule-II land and there being no allegation or evidence to the effect that anybody disputed the title of the defendant No. 1 in the schedule-II property and the plaintiff was prevented by anybody or threatened with dispossession from the schedule-II land, both the courts below ought to have considered the evidences both oral and documentary in record. 

 He submits that in the absence of any allegation of fraud in obtaining the deed of exchange, under the terms and condition of impugned deed the same is not at all liable to be cancelled, moreover, the plaintiff did not seek a declaration of title and has given boundary of the property in the plaint for specification, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed on that counts also. 

 It is also submitted that Erfan Uddin Chowdhury, one of the sons of plaintiff, Fayez Ahmed Chowdhury as constituted attorney of the plaintiff deposed in the suit before the trial court and represented the plaintiff respondent before the appellate court who after disposal of the appeal by a Nadabinama No. 1294 dated 03.04.2016 gave up his claim in the suit property, another son of the plaintiff named Fakhruddin Chowdhury by a registered deed No. 2024 dated 02.05.2016 transferred his share in schedule-II property to one Humayun Kabir son of Mahfuzul Islam, and one of the daughters of plaintiff named Jawhra Begum Chowdhury by a registered deed No. 5339 dated 18.07.2012 transferred her share in schedule-II property in favour of one Rezaul Karim admitting validity of deed of exchange in question and acquisition of title by inheritance from their father Fayez Ahmed Chowdhury and before fransfer all the heirs got their names mutated in khatian No. 1813 and by annexing all the three deeds, the petitioner filed an application for taking additional evidence and submits that those may be considered as additional evidences as nothing contrary could bring by the opposite party, meaning thereby, those documents are admitted by them.  In support of his submissions he has referred to a catena of cases: Noor Mohammad Khan and others vs. Government of Bangladesh and others reported in 42 DLR 434, Md. Zillur Rahman vs. Mst. Hosne Ara Begum reported in XII ADC, 338, Abu Naser Mohammad Wahidun Nabi and another vs. Md. Balai Roy and others reported in 15 BLT (AD) 27, Md. Naimuddin Sarder vs. Md. Abdul Kalam Biswas reported in 39  DLR (AD) 237, Md. Sorboddi Miah vs. Md. Serajul Haque and another reported in XII ADC 413, Kanchan Mallik and others vs. Saleha Begum and others reported in 9 ALR (AD) 115, Ratan Chandra Dey and others vs. Jinnator Nahar and others reported in 13 MLR (AD) 168 and Kanchan Mala Bepari Vs. Ananta Kumar Bepari & others reported in 6 DLR 254. 

 Mr. Taposh Kumar Dutta, learned advocate appearing for the Added Opposite Party No. 3, Md. Rianul Haque against whom no rule was issued, submits that after disposal of the appeal and pendency of this revision the Plaintiff Fayez Ahmed Chowdhury by a registered deed of gift No. 929 dated 06.04.2007 gifted the suit schedule-I property to the added opposite party No. 3 as grandson and after making gift in his favour all the rights, title and interest devolved upon him and he is the right person to defend the rule as principal opposite party. 

 He argued that the trial court as well as the appellate court concurrently observed and found that the defendant No. 1 had no title and possession in the suit property to be exchanged with Fayez Ahmed Chowdhury and as per terms and conditions of deed of exchange, the defendant could not deliver possession of the schedule-II property and could not produce any papers or documents showing that after purchase of the schedule-II property she got her name mutated in the khatian, paid rents to the government and also failed to prove delivery of possession to the plaintiff by giving specific boundary of the schedule-II property. Referring to Article 91 of the Limitation Act he submits that this is a suit for cancellation of deed of exchange and recovery of possession which is guided by Article 144 of the Limitation Act, providing 12 years of limitation, accordingly, the suit was filed within 12 years as provided in Article 144 of the Limitation Act and Article 91 prescribed three years limitation from the facts known to the plaintiff requiring cancellation of the deed and in the instant suit the plaintiff categorically stated in the plaint that the plaintiff on 20.12.1996 along with the witnesses mentioned in paragraph 8 of the plaint went to the house of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and demanded possession of the exchanged property, in the alternative to pay market price of the property and being refused by the defendants on 25.12.1996, the plaintiff has become compelled to file the present suit on 27.02.1997, within three years as provided in Article 91 of Limitation Act and both the courts below concurrently found that the suit is not barred by limitation. 

 He further submits that the defendant No. 1 could not prove by producing any document that she had title in the property, or she got possession of the property after purchase by giving definite boundary with specification. Both the courts below while decreeing the suit and disallowing the appeal concurrently found that in the deed of the defendant No. 1 dated 14.06.1984 as well as in the deed of exchange dated 13.03.1985 no boundary of the schedule-II property has been mentioned. In the absence of any boundary in the deeds, mutation in the khatian after purchase and payment of rents to the government she acquired no title and possession in the schedule-II property to be exchanged, resultantly, the defendant failed to deliver possession of the exchanged property to the plaintiff and handover all the title deeds in original, as such, both the courts below rightly held that title of the defendant in schedule-II property is defective which calls for cancellation of the deed in question. 

 It is also argued that in a suit for cancellation of any document there is no need for seeking declaration of title of the plaintiff and giving any boundary in the schedule to the plaint. He further submits that concurrent findings of both the courts below cannot be disturbed in revision unless the petitioners can show there is any misreading and non-appreciation of evidence both oral and documentary, misconstruction of law and non-consideration of any important document, but in the instant case the petitioner could show nothing as such, the Rule is liable to be discharged. In support of his submissions he has referred the cases of Shamshad Ali Shah and others vs. Syed Hassan Shan and others reported in LEX/SCPK/0012/194 Supreme Court of Pakistan and Kanchan Mala vs. Ananta Kumar Bepari and others reported in 6 DLR 254. 

 Mrs. Fawzia Karim Firoze with Mr. Khandaker Aminul Haque, learned Advocates appearing for the opposite party Nos. 1(ii)(a)-1(ii) 1(iii), 1(iv), 1(v), 1(vi), 1(vii), 1(viii), 1(ix) and 1(x) adopting submissions of Mr. Taposh further submits that non-compliance of obligation on the part of the defendants by delivery of possession of the exchanged property and title document in original to the plaintiff vitiated the whole purpose of the exchange deed calling for cancellation of the same. 

 She further argued that the suit is not barred by limitation because of the fact that for cancellation of a deed entire facts stated in the plaint have to be considered which entitles a person requiring cancellation of the deed and the plaintiff specifically and clearly stated in the plaint that the defendant on various pleas took time to deliver possession to the plaintiff and finally refused to the demand in the year 1996 and the suit was filed on 27.02.1997 within two months from the date of refusal, as such, the suit is not barred by limitation under Article 91 of the Limitation Act. 

 Admittedly, schedule-I property belonged to Fayez Ahmed Chowdhury, who exchanged the same with defendant No. 1 taking schedule-II property by a deed of exchange No. 1756 dated 13.03.1985 (exhibit-Cha and exhibit-2). It is also not denied that defendant No. 1 was in possession of schedule-I property as permissive possessor since 1967 and subsequently, on the basis of an agreement executed by plaintiff Fayez Ahmed Chowdhury in her favour dated 07.10.1974 and continued possession of the same till execution of deed of exchange on 13.03.1985. The plaintiff in his plaint claimed that on the following day of execution of deed of exchange, defendant No. 1 was supposed to deliver possession of the property to the plaintiff and handover all the title documents relating to schedule-II property, but the defendant on various pretext failed to deliver possession of the schedule-II property and related title document to the plaintiff. Thereafter, the plaintiff on several occasions requested the defendant and demanded possession of the schedule-II property. Since the defendant was delaying delivery of possession of schedule-II property, the plaintiff apprehended about title of the defendant No. 1 in the property and came to know that the defendant Nos. 1 and 2, misrepresenting the plaintiff and taking advantage of his good faith exchanged the schedule-II property with the schedule-I property of the plaintiff having no title at all, consequently, the defendants failed to deliver possession of the schedule-II property on repeated demands. Finally, he went to the house of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 with the witnesses on 20.12.1996 and demanded delivery of possession of the schedule-II property, in the alternative to pay market price of the property to the plaintiff, but the defendants through their relatives informed the plaintiff on 25.12.1996 that they will not deliver possession of the property and handover title documents to him. 

 The trial court observed that schedule-II property under B.S. khatian No. 608, plot No. 2246 measuring 1.24 acres originally belonged to Jamal Uddin and others from whom brother of the defendant No. 1 named Md. Shawkat Alam purchased the same by registered deed Nos. 5609 and 5610 both dated 08.11.1978 (exhibits-‘Gha’ and ‘Gha-2’). Thereafter, Shawkat Alam by a registered deed No. 4828 dated 14.06.1984 transferred 10 sataks of land to his sister defendant No. 1 (exhibit-‘Umo’), without any boundary to the schedule specifying the property sold, moreover, both of them did not get their names mutated in the khatian and paid rents to the government and for those reasons the defendant No. 1 acquired no title in the schedule-II land and also observed that none of the D.Ws. could prove that the defendant No. 1 delivered possession of schedule-II property to the plaintiff but curiously enough to mention that it is not the case of the plaintiff that anybody raised any objection about title of defendant No. 1 or his brother Shawkat Alam in the schedule-II property or the plaintiff was threatened by any other persons with dispossession of the property or questioning title of the plaintiff in schedule-II land given by exchange, moreover, DW4 has deposed saying delivery of possession to the plaintiff. Mere absence of boundary in a sale deed, absence of mutation in the name of the purchaser, non-payment of rents cannot make the defendant No. 1 titleless in the property. The trial court in a suit for cancellation of an exchange deed instead of finding the reasons and circumstances for cancellation of a deed tried to decide the matter of title of defendant No. 1 wrongly in the manner mentioned above. 

 Moreover, it is the definite case of the plaintiff that he was supposed to get delivery of possession of the property on the following day of execution of deed of exchange, i,e, on 14.03.1985 as stated in paragraph 3 of the plaint. It is not the case of the plaintiff that the deed was obtained by the defendants by practicing fraud or he came to know about fraud on 20.12.1996, the only allegation brought against the defendants is non-delivery of possession and title documents of the property to the plaintiff which cannot be construed in any way that the defendant No. 1 had no title in the schedule-II property. 

 The trial court further held that section 119 of the Transfer of Property Act entitles the plaintiff to get the deed of exchange cancelled by reason of any defect in the title of the other party deprived of the thing or any part of the thing received by him in exchange and herein, since the defendant No. 1 had no title in the property, the plaintiff rightly instituted the present suit and it is quite maintainable in the light of the decision report in 44 DLR (AD) 86 and on the above findings decreed the suit. The views taken by the trial court is not well founded. 

 “If any party to an exchange or any person claiming through or under such party is by reason of any defect in the title of the other party deprived of the thing or any part of the thing received by him in exchange, then, unless a contrary intention appears from the terms of the exchange, such other party is liable to him or any person claiming through or under him for loss caused thereby, or at the option of the person so deprived, for the return of the thing transferred, if still in the possession of such other party or his legal representative or a transferee from him without consideration.” 

 As per terms of the exchange, the plaintiff is entitled to claim market price of the property prevailing at that time along with compensation, by reason of any defect in title of the defendant No. 1 in schedule-II property but the plaintiff is not entitled to get the deed of exchange cancelled or return of the property, moreover, in the present suit the plaintiff could not prove any defect in the title of the defendant No. 1 in schedule-II land. 

 The appellate court while disallowing the appeal nothing held and observed new other than the observations made by the trial court. The appellate court also concurrently observed that for absence of boundary in the schedule to the deed of the defendant No. 1, absence of mutation in the name of Shawkat Alam as well as in the name of defendant No. 1 and non-payment of rents to the government proved that the defendant No. 1 had no title and possession in the schedule-II property to be exchanged with the plaintiff and also found that the suit is not barred by limitation under Article 91 of the Limitation Act as well as the plaintiff is entitled to get the deed of exchange cancelled under section 119 of the Transfer of Property Act. 

 In the case of Kanchan Mala Bepari vs. Ananta Kumar Bepari, 6 DLR 254, the question raised primarily on limitation and maintainability of suit. It was filed after 15 years claiming that the deed dated 14.12.1925 was a void and fraudulent document and for a declaration that said document was a Jaisudi mortgage and it has been extinguished by lapse of 15 years from the date of the bond. So, question is when the period of limitation begins to run. Here the plaintiff stated that he executed the deed on good faith believing that the defendant No. 1 has title over the property and she will deliver possession of the same, but in the year 1996 he came to know that the defendant No. 1 had no title. Both the courts below concurrently held that because of absence of boundary in the schedule to the deed of the year 1984, in the exchange deed, absence of mutation in the name of defendant No. 1, non-payment of rents to the government, the defendant No. 1 acquired no title in schedule-II property, such observations are not correct in view of the established principles of law that title transferred to the transferee with the deed and non-payment of rent does not affect the title as held in the cases of Abdun Noor and others vs. Aziruddin and others, reported in 21 BLT (AD) 161 and Abdul Mannan Bhuiya and others vs. Md. Nasir Hossain and others reported in 18 BLC(AD) 44, observing that “the registered document prevail upon record of right. S.A. and R.S. records were not an evidence of title and that a registered document would prevail upon the records of rights and remain in force unless the same was concelled by an appropriate civil court.” 

 In the schedule to the plaint, there is no specific boundary to identify from which portion of the suit plot the plaintiff prayed for khas possession where the trial court criticized the boundary contain in the schedule-I of the property in the exchange deed to be vague and confusing. Plaintiff having failed to comply with the mandatory requirement of law in giving clear description or boundary to indentify the suit land, is not entitled to any decree for defect in the plaint as held in the case of Md. Sorboddi Miah vs. Md. Serajul Haque and another, reported in 12 ADC 413 and Noor Mohammad Khan and others vs. Bangladesh and others, reported in 42 DLR 435. 

 In the cases of Ratan Chandra Dey and others vs. Jinnator Nahar and others, reported in 13 MLR (AD) 168, Sanjib Kumar Bose and another vs. Syed Shamsuddin Ahmed and another, reported in 1 BCR (AD) 273, Mst. Sahara Khatun and another vs. Mst. Anwara Khatun and others, reported in 1 BCR (1981) 126 held that, a suit for cancellation and declaration that the deed of exchange is fraudulent, not binding upon the plaintiff is not maintainable without declaration of title. The present case also filed by the plaintiff without declaration of his title in the suit property. 

 In Nasimuddin Mia vs. Manindra Kumar Maloo and others case, the plaintiff filed the suit for cancellation of an exchange deed by which defendant No. 1 got schedule-1 property in Bangladesh in exchange of schedules-2 and 3 property in Assam, subsequently, the plaintiff came to know that the defendant No. 1 had no title in schedules-2 and 3 property as he fransferred the property earlier, hence practiced fraud, but in the present case no allegation of fraud has been alleged and proved. Facts stated in the plaint and evidence led cannot constitute any fraud and defect of title of the defendant No. 1 in the schedule-II property. Therefore, application of provision of Article-91 of the Limitation Act, depends on the fact of each individual cases like the present one. 

 During hearing of the Rule, the petitioner filed an application for taking additional evidence annexing some documents praying for accepting those as additional evidence which are mutation khatian No.1813 in the name of heirs of original plaintiff Fayez Ahmed Chowdhury (though the opposite parties without any proof claimed that subsequently, this mutation khatian was cancelled), true copy of deed No. 5339 dated 18.07.2012 executed by Alhaj Jawhra Begum daughter of the plaintiff in favour of one Rezaul Karim, sale deed No. 2024 dated 02.05.2016 executed by Fakhruddin Chowdhury son of the plaintiff infavour of one Humayun Kabir transferring their shares in plot No. 2246, schedule-II to the deed of exchange and plaint, admitting validity of the exchange deed dated 13.03.1985 and Deed of Disclaimer No. 1294 dated 03.04.2016 executed by Erfan Uddin Chowdhury son of Fayez Ahmed Chowdhury relinquishing his title in the schedule-I land to the deed of exchange and plaint in favour of defendant No. 1 who represented and deposed in the suit as attorney of original plaintiff Fayez Ahmed Chowdhury. 

 Now, the question has come, had the deed of exchange not acted upon and possession of schedule-II property not delivered to Fayez Ahmed Chowdhury and the defendant No. 1 had no title in the property to be exchanged with Fayez Ahmed Chowdhury how the daughter and sons of Fayez Ahmed Chowdhury, after his death can transfer the property to other persons admitting validity of the exchange deed and delivered possession of their share in the land to the purchasers Rezaul Karim and Humayun Kabir, but all those documents are found to be executed and registered after disposal of the appeal by the appellate court and during pendency of the present Rule which did not enter into evidence by way of additional written statement or producing any witness. To give specific findings on long waiting of the plaintiff coupled with law of limitation, maintainability of the present suit and validity of deed of exchange and for proper adjudication of the matter in dispute legal effect and consequences of subsequent incidences and events occurred, as appearing from those deeds are required to be taken into consideration. In that view of the matter it requires recording of evidence to bring those documents on record. 

 It is true that any transfer by any party during pendency of any suit is hit by section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, but in the instant case the situation is otherwise, here the transfers made by the claimants of schedule-1 property in suit, not by the defendant. In the absence of proper adjudication of the whole matter in dispute, transfers made by the heirs of original plaintiff Fayez Ahmed Chowdhury will give rise to multiplicity of proceedings. To avoid multiplicity of proceedings and to get the dispute effectively adjudicated for all intents and purposes, this court thinks that for the interest of justice the suit is required to be sent back on remand to the appellate court to consider and record additional evidence affording the appellant petitioner an opportunity to file additional written statement and to adduce evidence in respect of documents filed and the Respondent-opposite parties shall get opportunity to cross examine the witnesses adduced, accordingly, application for taking additional evidence is allowed. 

 The appellate court should give clear findings in the light of the observations made in the body of the judgment on the point of (i) legal position of the period spent from 1985-1996 under Article 91 of the Limitation Act, (ii) application of section 119 of the Transfer of Property Act in the present case (iii) whether the situations stated in the plaint can call for cancellation of deed of exchange under the terms and conditions contain therein (iv) consequences of transfers made by the plaintiff by a gift and transfers made by his heirs to third parties and (v) maintainability of suit on the point of limitation, want of prayer for declaration of title and absence of boundary in the schedule to the plaint.

parties:
Md. Kamal Hossain and others ------- Appellants.
Vs.
Abdul Ahad and others --------- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Hasan Foez Siddique, C. J: This appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 22.08.2007 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1542 of 2001 making the Rule absolute upon setting aside the judgment and decree dated 27.09.2000 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 7th Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 34 of 2000 reversing those dated 14.11.1999 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, 5th Additional Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 180 of 1997. 

 The relevant facts, for disposal of this appeal, in short, are that Azizan Bibi, predecessor-in-interest of the respondent No.1, filed the aforesaid suit for cancellation of document, declaration of decree not binding and recovery of khas possession of the suit land along with declaration of title to the same stating that the Government leased out the suit land for 99 years and delivered possession of the same to one Md. Hasib who sold it to plaintiff Azizan Bibi by registered deed of sale bearing No.3399 dated 01.04.1964. Defendant No.1 entered into the suit land as a tenant in the month of June/July, 1965 and at the beginning of the liberation war defendant No.1 terminated the tenancy and left the house. Just after liberation of Bangladesh, defendant No.1 forcefully took over possession of the case house and drove out the plaintiff therefrom and took her L.T.I.’s on some blank papers and managed to receive the documents of the house from the plaintiff and thereafter finding no other alternative, she took shelter in the Geneva Camp and she had been living there. Thereafter, while she had been living in the Geneva Camp, defendant No.1 again took her L.T.I’s on some blank and written papers. The Government declared the case house as an abandoned building. The plaintiff filed Case No.80 of 1989 in the First Court of Settlement for exclusion of the same from the list of abandoned buildings. Defendant No.1 also filed case No.81 of 1989 in the said Court and those two cases were heard analogously. The Court of Settlement allowed both the cases by a common judgment and order dated 15.08.1995. At the time of hearing of those cases it was revealed that defendant Nos.1-2 as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No.1339 of 1981 for declaration of title and recovery of possession of the case house against the Government of Bangladesh in the Fourth Court of the learned Joint District Judge, Dhaka and, subsequently, it was re-numbered as Title Suit No.909 of 1985 on transfer to the Second Court of the learned Joint District Judge, who, upon conclusion of hearing was pleased to decree the suit ex parte on 02.03.1991. Government of Bangladesh filed Miscellaneous Case No.100 of 1991 for setting aside the ex parte decree, but it was dismissed on contest on 30.04.1991, and thereafter, the Government preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No.112 of 1992, which was also dismissed on 11.06.1995. The plaintiff was not impleaded in that suit who came to know definitely about the story of purchase deed dated 23.10.1979 on 24.10.1995 by obtaining certified copy of the same. The deed of sale dated 23.10.1979 is void, ineffective, fraudulent and without consideration. The plaintiff is an old pardanshin illiterate lady and defendant No.1 fraudulently created the deed of sale in respect of the case house. She did not receive any consideration from defendant Nos.1-2. The cause of action of the suit arose on 15.08.1995 when defendant No.1 produced the aforesaid deed of purchase in the Court of Settlement. During the pendency of the suit the plaintiff died leaving respondent No.1 as her legal heir, who was substituted in the suit. 

 The defendant Nos.1-2 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement contending inter alia that the Government leased out the case house for 99 years and delivered possession of the same to one Md. Hasib by registered deed of lease dated 25.11.1963. He sold the case house and delivered possession of the house to plaintiff Azizan Bibi, mother of respondent No.1. Said Azizan Bibi transferred the case house to defendant Nos. 1-2 at a consideration of tk.20,000/- by deed of sale bearing No.5095 dated 23.10.1979 and delivered possession of the same to them on the same day. She appeared before the Sub-Registrar and put her L.T.I. in the deed of sale and in the L.T.I. register of the S.R. Office upon receiving consideration money from defendants Nos.1-2 in presence of witnesses. Azizan Bibi also handed over the original title deeds of the case house to defendant Nos.1-2 on the same day. They had been living in the case house since 23.10.1979 but the Government and its officials were disturbing the defendant Nos.1-2, hence they were constrained to institute Title Suit No.1339 of 1981 for declaration of title in the case property against the Government in the Fourth Court of Joint District Judge, Dhaka in 1981. Ministry of Housing and Public Works issued a notice to defendant Nos.1-2 to surrender possession of the house to them on 24.08.1982, and thereafter, defendant Nos.1-2 were evicted by Police force from the case house on 30.08.1982. Then defendant Nos. 1-2 amended the plaint of the suit and prayed for recovery of khas possession of the suit property and it was allowed by the Court. Title Suit No.1339 of 1981 was renumbered as Title Suit No.909 of 1985 on transfer to the Court of the learned Joint District Judge, Second Court, Dhaka who upon hearing was pleased to decree the suit ex parte on 02.03.1991. The decree holders Nos.1-2 filed Title Execution Case No.05 of 1991 in the said Court and possession of the suit land was restored to defendant Nos.1-2 by the learned Joint District Judge, Dhaka on 14.10.1991. The Government filed Miscellaneous Case No.100 of 1991 for setting aside the ex parte decree and it was dismissed on contest, and thereafter, the Government preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No.112 of 1992 in the Court of the learned District Judge and it was also dismissed on 11.06.1995. 

 Mr. Alim Hossain (appearing with the leave of the Court) appearing for the appellants, submits that Azizan Bibi executed the sale deed, hence she could not claim the sale deed to be void and thereafter, this suit was barred under Article 6 of P.O. No.16 of 1972.  After exclusion of the suit property from the list of abandoned building by virtue of the judgment and order of the Court of Settlement, she was barred by the principle of estoppel, and therefore, the judgment and order of the High Court Division is liable to be set aside.  He submits that plaintiff Azizan Bibi was admittedly out of possession from the suit land for more than 25 years, so her prayer for recovery of khas possession of the same was barred by limitation. He further submits that as per the decree of Title Suit No.909 of 1985, the possession of the case property was restored to the appellant and the Court of Settlement allowed the settlement case in their favour. Since the Court of Settlement released the property in favour of appellants, the instant case was not hit by the provision of P.O. No.16 of 1972. 

 On the other hand, Mr. A. J.Mohmmad Ali, learned Senior Counsel, appearing for the respondent No.1, submits that the suit property was enlisted as abandoned property under P.O. No.16 of 1972 and the same was under the control and management of the Government till 14.10.1991 as per the admission of defendant- appellant, and the impugned deed dated 23.10.1979 and the ex parte decree  dated 02.03.1991 were null ex parte decree and void in view of Article 6 of P.O.16 of 1972, therefore, the appeal is liable to be dismissed. He further submits that admittedly the plaintiff was lawful owner of the property and after the war of liberation she took shelter in Geneva Camp, Mohammadpur, Dhaka to save her life and the property was enlisted as an abandoned property under  P.O. No.16 of 1972 and that property was under the control and management of the Government  through Government allottee Md. Hanif till 14.10.1991 and the defendant -appellant took over possession of the said property on 14.10.1991 through Court on the basis of the impugned deed dated 23.10.1979 and the ex parte decree dated 02.03.1991. The plaintiff was not party to the decree and that Court of Settlement released the property on 15.08.1995 and the plaintiff came to know about the disputed deed and decree from the record of Court of Settlement which delivered judgment on 15.8.1995 and the instant suit was filed on 27.4.1996 which was within time, therefore, the High Court Division rightly decreed the suit. He lastly submits that the impugned deed and the ex parte decree obtained by the defendant appellants are products of fraud and that the plaintiff was not a party to the said ex parte decree and her title in property  has not been lost by the said ex parte decree and that said decree is not binding upon the plaintiff, the High Court Division rightly decreed the suit. 

 It appears from the materials on record that Azizan Bibi instituted the instant suit stating that the Government allotted the suit plot to one Md. Hasib on 25.11.1963, who sold the same to plaintiff Azizan Bibi by the deed dated 01.04.1964. It is the case of the plaintiff that  the defendant took  her L.T.I. on a blank paper on gun point and compelled her to leave the house and, thus, she took shelter in Geneva Camp and, thereafter, the suit house was enlisted as abandoned property under P.O. No.16 of 1972 and the said property was enlisted as abandoned property in the Government published official gazette in 1986 and plaintiff filed Settlement Case No.80 of 1989 before the Court of Settlement for getting the said property released. On the other hand, defendant No.1, predecessor-in-interest of the present appellants, filed Settlement Case No.81 of 1989 for getting the said property released claiming that he obtained the suit property on the basis of kabla deed dated 23.10.1979 and also obtained ex parte decree in Title Suit No.1339 of 1981 and got possession through Court on 14.10.1991. The claim of the plaintiff was that the said kabla deed and decree were products of fraud and those were null and void. 

 Since the plaintiff instituted the suit for cancellation of deed dated 23.10.1979, it is the duty of the plaintiff to prove that the sale deed was obtained fraudulently. It appears that the High Court Division treated the said deed void assuming that the defendant appellants purchased the said land when the property was declared as abandoned property. Therefore, such transfer was null and void. The trial Court as well as High Court Division in their judgments  did not draw any such conclusion that plaintiff Azizan Bibi did not execute the kabla deed dated 23.10.1979, though it was the case of the plaintiff that defendant No.1 obtained her signatures on blank papers  and created the kabla deed dated 23.10.1979. In the plaint, the plaintiff, inter alia, stated, "বাংলাদেশ স্বাধীন হবার পর "ক" তপসিল বর্নিত সম্পত্তিতে ১নং বিবাদী ও আরো কিছু লোক জোরপূর্বক প্রবেশ করিয়া প্রানের ভয় দেখাইয়া কিছু অলিখিত কাগজে জোর পূর্বক বাদিনীর টিপ নিয়াছিল। পরবর্তীতে বাদিনী জেনেভা ক্যাম্পে একাকী থাকাকালীন সময়ে ১নং বিবাদী তঞ্চকতামুলে কিছু লিখিত ও অলিখিত কাগজে এই বলে বাদিনীর টিপ নেয় যে বাদিনীর তাহার নালিশী সম্পত্তি ফেরৎ পাওয়ার জন্য ঐ সমস্ত কাগজে বাদিনীর টিপসহি দরকার। টিপসহি নেবার পর ১নং বিবাদী বাদিনীকে এই মর্মে ভয় দেখাইয়াছে যে, এই টিপ সহির কথা অন্য কাহারও নিকট প্রকাশ করিলে ১নং বিবাদী বাদিনী এবং তাহার ছেলে মেয়েদেরকে প্রানে মারিয়া ফেলিবে। এমতাবস্হায় ১-২নং বিবাদীর অনুকুলে বাদিনী দত্তা মর্মে প্রকাশিত বিগত ২৩-১০-১৯৭৯ইং তারিখের সম্মাদিত ও রেজিষ্ট্রিকৃত নালিশী কবালা দলিল পন প্রবৃত্তিহীন তঞ্চকী, ফেরারী, ফল ও বলবিহীন এবং নিম্নোক্ত হেতুতে রদ যোগ্য বটে।" The plaintiff brought the allegation that defendant No.1 managed to get the kabla deed executed and registered by practising fraud, but none of the Court drew any conclusion that the plaintiff has been able to prove the allegation of fraud. Since the Kabla deed dated 23.10.1979 was executed and registered, it is to be presumed that all the official acts were done accordingly. It was the plaintiff’s duty to prove fraud which has not been done in the instant case. It further appears from the judgment and order passed by the Court of Settlement dated 15.08.1995 in Settlement Case No.80 of 1989 and 81 of 1989 that it was held that the property should not have been included in the list of abandoned properties and it ordered that the property was liable to be excluded from ‘Ka’ schedule of the abandoned building. It further appears from the materials on record that before publication of the property in the official gazette in 1986 in the list of the abandoned properties, the defendant Nos.1-2 instituted Title Suit No.1339 of 1981, in the 4th Court of the then Subordinate Judge, Dhaka against Government claiming the property on the basis of  kabla deed  dated 23.10.1979 (the said suit was renumbered as Title Suit No.909 of 1985 in the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka) and for declaration that the claim of the  Government that the suit property is abandoned property was illegal and also for recovery of khas possession. They added the prayer for recovery of possession after Government had dispossessed them from suit land on 30.08.1982. The said suit was decreed on 02.03.1991 and upon execution of the said decree they took possession of the same, that is, the present plaintiff Azizan Bibi had no possession in the suit land and she did not take any step for getting the possession of the same. It appears from the judgment and order of the Court of settlement that Azizan Bibi never left this country and her whereabouts was not untraced. So inclusion of the property as abandoned property was not justified. Azizan Bibi transferred her right and title in the suit land to defendant Nos.1-2 by virtue of kabla deed dated 23.10.1979 and we have found that there is no finding of the Court below that defendant No.1 obtained the said deed by practising fraud, therefore, the right and title of Azizan Bibi to the suit land has been extinguished after execution and registration of the sale deed dated 23.10.1979 and by virtue of the said deed her title to the suit land has been divested to defendant Nos.1-2. 

 It appears from the judgment and order of Court of Settlement that it opined that the property was wrongly included in the list of abandoned properties and Azizan Bibi and defendant No.1 can settle their dispute in competent Court. Since after execution and registration of sale deed dated 23.10.1979 Azizan Bibi lost her title to the suit land and that she failed to prove that the impugned deed was fraudulent one, we are of the view that plaintiff Azizan Bibi has no title to the suit land, the High Court Division has committed an error of law in making the Rule absolute thereby decreeing the suit.

parties:
Masud Miah alias Masud Karim (Md) and others---------Petitioners
Vs
Shoilanda Chandra Mudak---------Opposite party
full_judgment:
Md Riaz Uddin Khan J: By this Rule the opposite party no. 1 was asked to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 5-7-2017 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Kishoreganj in Civil Revision No. 68 of 2016 allowing the revision and thereby setting aside the order No. 27 dated 19-9-2016 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Kishoreganj in Title Suit No. 358 of 2015 (Partition) allowing the application under Rule 13A of Order IX of the Code of Civil Procedure filed by the petitioners should not be set-aside. 

 2. At the time of issuance of Rule the operation of the judgment and decree dated 21-8-2016 (decree signed on 22-8-2016) passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Kishoreganj in Title Suit No. 358 of 2015 (Partition) was stayed and the parties were directed to maintain status quo in respect of possession of the suit land. 

 3. The short facts for disposal of this Revisional Application in brief is that the Opposite Party No. I as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 358 of 2015 (Partition) in the Court of learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Kishoreganj against the father of the present petitioners and the Opposite Party No. 6 as Defendant No. 1 and the Opposite Parties Nos. 2-5 as Defendant Nos. 2-5 for partition of the suit land. 

 4. It is admitted position that the Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 did not appear before the trial court and only Defendant No. 5, the Government appeared and by filing written statement contested the suit. The learned trail court after hearing the plaintiff and the Defendant No. 5 decreed the suit by its judgment and decree dated 21-8-2016 (decree signed on 22-8-2016). Thereafter being informed about the said decree the present petitioners as the legal heirs of Defendant No. 1 filed an application under Rule 13A of Order IX of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex-party decree passed against them and to restore the original Title Suit. After hearing the parties the learned trail court allowed the application by its order dated 19-9-2016 on condition to pay Taka 3,000 (three thousand) as cost. Against that order dated 19-9-2016 the plaintiff filed Revisional Application before the District Judge, Kishoreganj, which was ultimately heard by the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Kishoreganj. After hearing both the parties the learned Additional District Judge, by his impugned judgment and order dated 5-7-2017 allowed the Revisional application on the finding that the trail court was wrong in allowing the application filed under Rule 13A of Order IX of the Code of Civil Procedure as it was admitted position that the predecessor of the applicants did not appear before the trail court by filing Vokalatnama or did not file written statement. 

 6. On the other hand Mr Md Hamidur Rahman, the learned advocate appeared on behalf of the Opposite Party No. 1 and filed counter affidavit. He submits that the trail court did not at all apply his judicial mind and he failed to consider that the application filed by the petitioners were not supported by any affidavit rather there was verification. He next submits that under rule 13A of order IX there is no "Scope for any defendants who did not appear before the court and filed written statement to file any application for setting aside the ex-parte decree and for restoration of the original suit. In the instant case it is admitted position that the petitioners or their predecessor did not appear and file written statement in the trail court. Allowing the application filed under rule 13A of order IX the trial court committed serious error of law and the lower Revisional Court correctly allowed the Revision on consideration of legal point. Any non-appearing defendants may have other remedies available in the Code of Civil Procedure but not under rule 13 A of order IX of the Code of Civil Procedure. The learned Advocate for the opposite party prays for discharging the Rule with cost.
