parties:
Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Works, Bangladesh and others.......Petitioners
vs
Md Tariq Sultan and others……….Respondents
full_judgment:
3. Writ petitioner-respondent Md Tariq Sultan, through his constituted power-of-attorneys, filing the instant writ petition, challenged the notification of enlistment of the property mentioned in Serial No. 34 at page No. 9762(8), Plot No.388, New Eskaton Road (hereinafter referred as disputed property) in the 'Ka' list of the abandoned properties vide Bangladesh Gazette dated 23-9-1986 as per provision of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 (Ordinance LIV of 1985) and obtained Rule. His case, in short, was that the disputed property originally belonged to Ali Mohammad son of Mohammad Jawad Ispahani who got the same by virtue of the sale deeds No.4196 and 4197 dated 8-6-1951. Ali Mohammad transferred the said property to the writ petitioner by a registered sale deed dated 21-4-1955 and delivered possession. In SA operation, the same was recorded in the name of the writ petitioner in Khatian No.382. In RS operation, the same was also recorded in the name of the writ petitioner. In March 2001, the writ petitioner went to collect city jarip khatian of the disputed property and came to know that the disputed property had been enlisted in the 'Ka' list of the abandoned properties. The writ petitioner went to the Court of Settlement for taking step to get the same released but the Court of Settlement did not accept the writ petitioner's prayer since the same was time barred. Thus, the writ petitioner filed the writ petition. 

 4. The Government appeared in the Rule and contested the same contending that the papers produced by the writ petitioners are forged, created and fraudulent. The original owner Md Tariq Sultan left this country during the war of liberation and he was found untraced. Accordingly, the Government took over possession of the said property treating the same as abandoned property as per provision of Article 4 of the PO 16 of 1972. The power of attorney as allegedly executed by Md Tariq Sultan is fraudulent one. The Government has been possessing the said property through its lessee. The Rule should be discharged. 

 11. The writ petitioner produced the photostat copy of his National Identity Card (Annexure-A) which shows that the date of birth and ID number were hand-written. Peculiar aspect is that the digit mentioned in the ID card encroached its border which is unusual. The signature of the Md Tariq Sultan is not visible. Annexure-A1 shows that the same is a citizenship certificate which has been issued by the penal Mayor of Bogra Municipality and address of the writ petitioner has been mentioned as Thonthonia Sufipara, Ward No.12, Bogra. Annexure A-2, birth certificate issued by Bogra Municipality, shows thal Md Tariq Sultan was born on 3-6-1933 but from the photostat copy of the deed dated 21-1-1955 produced before the Court it appears that Mohammad Tariq Sultan was shown as minor inasmuch as according to birth certificate, at the relevant time, Mohammad Tariq Sultan was aged about 22 years. From Annexure A-3 certificate issued by the panel Mayor of Bogra Municipality it appears that late Sultan Mirza son of late Gazi Sultan died leaving only heir, namely, Md Tariq Sultan. That is, his grand father used the title 'Gazi' and father used the title 'Mirza'. From annexure 'B' the photostat copy of the certified copy of deed executed on 21-4-1955 it appears that recipient of the deed was Mohammad Tariq Sultan minor son Mr Sultan of No.63/2 Purana Paltan, Police Station-Lalbagh, Dhaka. It is not the case of the writ petitioner Md Tareque Sultan that when he was minor, he came to Dhaka froth Thanthania, Bogra and started residing at No.63/2 Purana Paltan, Lalbag, Dhaka and purchased 1 bigha 11/2 chattaks of land of New Eskaton, Ramna Dhaka. It is not the case of the writ petitioner that his father purchased the disputed property in his name, that is, he was the benamder of his father. It appears from Annexure G and G-1 that on 20-12-2012 and 11-3-2013 aforesaid three persons, namely, Rashed Zahid, Firoza Begum and Shamsunnahar, on behalf of Tarique Sultan, filed two separate applications addressing the Secretary, Ministry of Housing and Public Works for getting release of the disputed property from the list of abandoned properties. Annexure-1 shows that on 3-3-2014 those three persons swearing an affidavit before the Notary Public, Dhaka declared that Tarique Sultan filed an application on 2-3-2014 before the First Court of Settlement, Dhaka along with the prayer for condonation of delay for getting release of the disputed property inasmuch as in paragraph 7 of the writ petition it was stated that in the month of March 2001 the petitioner collected the City Jorip Khatian and came to know that the property has been included in the list of abandoned properties and, upon query, he found that the case property has been enlisted in the 'Ka' list of the abandoned buildings published in the official gazette dated 23-9-1986 at page No.9762(8) serial No. 34. Annexure-1, the photostat copy of the certified copy of the power of attorney allegedly executed by Tarique Sultan in favour of those three persons it appears that father of Ali Mohammad, the executant of the deed dated 21-4-1955, is “মোহাম্মদ জাবেদ টিপানী” inasmuch as the name of Ali Mohammed was Mohammad Jawad Ispahani. 

 13. It is a fit case for holding an elaborate inquiry to find out the actual culprits who are involved in this fraudulent attempt. The writ petitioner never produced the original title deeds before the Court for perusal. It is apparent that they fraudulently used some instruments for weighing which they know to be false. 

 14. The aforesaid facts clearly questioned the identity of the writ petitioner. Though the papers produced in the High Court Division were highly doubtful, the High Court Division, ignoring t:iose aspects, erroneously believing the papers (though original documents were not produced) released the property, in question.
case_type_name: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal

parties:
Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh Meherpur -------- Defendant-Appellant-Petitioner
VS
Abdul Bari Shah and others --------- Plaintiff-Respondent-Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
The Rules issued calling upon the Opposite party Nos. 1 & 2 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 12-11-2008 and 18-11-2008 respectively passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Meherpur in Title Appeal No. 68 of 1999 affirming those of dated 24-2-1999 and 28-2-1999 respectively passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Meherpur Sadar, Meherpur in Title Suit No. 326 of 1995 decreeing the suit should not be set-aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

 2. The facts leading to the issuance of Rule in a nutshell can be stated thus, the present opposite party Nos. 1 & 2 as plaintiffs instituted the Original Title Suit No. 326 of 1995 in the court of learned Senior Assistant Judge, Meherpur Sadar, Meherpur for declaration of their title in the suit property and for a further declaration that the enlistment of the suit property as vested property is illegal, void and not binding upon the plaintiffs contending inter alia that the suit property originally belonged to one Gopi Dasi and the SA khatian No. 343 was correctly recorded in her name under mouja Chandpur of District Meherpur, comprising an area of 16 decimals of land. The owner of the property, Gopi Dasi by a registered kabala deed dated 4-2-1960 transferred the land in favour of one Mayzuddin and the purchaser Mayzuddin after mutation of his name started to pay rents to the Government. Subsequently, Mayzuddin transferred 6 decimals of land in favour of one Shawkat Ali and 5 decimals in favour of one Ruhul Amin. Out of the remaining 5 decimals of land Moyzuddin transferred 21/2 decimal in favour of the plaintiff No. 1 by a transfer deed dated 3-12-1973 AD and the rest 21/2 decimals of land was transferred in favour of the father of the Defendant No. 2 by Moyzuddin. The further case of the plaintiffs is such that the plaintiff No. 1 and the father of the plaintiff No. 2 also purchased 7 decimals of land from plot No. 1618 which is adjacent to the suit plot. The plaintiffs are possessing their purchased land jointly and mutated their names in the Government seresta and paying rents to the Government. They have erected their dwelling huts in the suit property and residing therein. In the suit property the plaintiffs have pacca building and in the preliminary stage of RS record, 12 decimals of land was recorded in the names of the plaintiff No. 1 and the father of the plaintiff No. 2. The father of plaintiff No. 2 died leaving behind five daughters, one wife and one son, the plaintiffs No. 2. The plaintiff No. 2 by a registered sub-kabala deed dated 16-4-1989 AD purchased the lands of other co-sharers measuring 06 decimals of land in the suit holding. On 28-2-1995 the plaintiffs going to the local Tahshil Office came to learn that the suit properly measuring 05 decimals of land has not been recorded finally in their names in the RS record and out of the suit property 1/2 decimals of land has been wrongly recorded in the name of defendant No. 2 in Plot No. 6036. The defendant No. 2 entered into a solenama with the plaintiffs for that portion of land. On the above mentioned date the concerned Tahshilder denied to accept rent from the plaintiffs, and thereafter the plaintiffs instituted the original suit. 

 3. The contrary case of the defendant No. 1, Government of Bangladesh is short is thus, that the suit property originally belonged to Gopi Dasi, who migrated to India prior to 1960 AD and started to reside therein since then and accordingly, under the operation of law, the property has become enemy property and subsequently as vested and non-resident property and that the RS record has been correctly prepared in the name of Government. The further case of the Government is such that the plaintiffs having no right, title, interest and possession in the suit property, on false allegations filed the suit which is liable to be dismissed. 

 4. The learned trial court during trial of the original suit after taking evidence from the sides of the respective parties decreed the suit on contest by the judgment and decree dated 24-2-1999. 

 5. Being aggrieved the defendant, Government has preferred a Title Appeal being No. 68 of 1999 in the court of the learned District Judge, Meherpur which was transmitted to the 2nd court of the learned Joint District Judge, Meherpur for hearing and disposal and the learned appellate court hearing the appeal disallowed the same affirming the judgment and decree passed by the trial court by the impugned judgment and decree dated 12-11-2008. 

 8. The learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits that the learned trial court as well as the appellate court during disposal of the original suit and its subsequent appeal committed illegality and irregularity. The learned Deputy Attorney-General (here in after DAG) submits that the original suit was not maintainable in its present form as it was barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and the law of limitation. The learned DAG also submits that the CS & SA recorded tenants of the suit property have migrated to India in 1965, without disposing the suit property in favour of any body in any manner and did not come back to this country and, as such, the suit property has been declared vested and non-resident property under Defence of Pakistan Rules, 1965 and the suit property has been enlisted in the census list of enemy property and the Government is possessing the suit property through their lessees. The learned DAG also submits that the plaintiffs have created some false and antedated documents, only to grab the Government's property and both the parties during trial have adduced evidences in support of their respective cases but the courts below without proper assessment of evidence and appreciation of law decided the merit of the suit in favour of the plaintiffs, resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned DAG lastly submits that the suit land has been assumed the character of the enemy property (vested property) in the period between 6-9-1965 and 16-2-1969 AD and thereby comes within the definition of enemy property (now vested property) under Rule 169 (4) of the Defence of Pakistan Rules, 1965 but the learned appellate court without considering that, decided the merit of the appeal against the appellant illegally and, as such, the impugned judgment and decree is not sustainable in law and facts. 

 9. As against the aforesaid submission of the learned DAG the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite parties opposing the Rule controverted the argument advanced from the side of the Government. The learned Advocate submits that, neither the trial court nor the appellate court during disposal of the original suit and its subsequent appeal committed any illegality and irregularity. The learned Advocate further submits that, during trial of the original suit by sufficient credible evidence, the plaintiffs have proved that the original owner of the property transferred the suit land along with other land measuring 16 decimals of land by a registered sub kabala deed dated 4-2-1960 in favour of one Moyzuddin and it is also proved that Moyzuddin mutated his name in the Government seresta and paid rent. The learned Advocate also submits that Moyzuddin subsequently transferred the land in favour of one Shawkat Ali and Ruhul Amin. The plaintiff No. 1 subsequently by a kabala deed dated 3-12-1973 purchased 21/2 decimals of land and by another sub-kabala deed of the same date Moyzuddin transferred 21/2 decimals of land in favour of the father of plaintiff No. 02 from the suit jote and by successive transfer deeds, in this way the plaintiff-opposite parties have acquired right, title, interest and possession in the suit property and the suit property never became enemy property or vested property under the ambit of enemy property laws inasmuch as prior to 1965 AD the admitted original owner of the property, Gopi Dasi transferred the suit property in favour of Moyzuddin and handed over possession. The learned Advocate submits that the defendant, Government in order to prove the case of their pleading's, did not adduce any oral or documentary evidence and, as such, the pleading's case of the Government remain disproved under the ambit of law. The learned Advocate in support of his contention referred some decisions of this court and our apex court reported in BCR (1988) 179, 50 DLR (AD) 70, 17 BLD 249 = 1 BLC 576 and 5 CLR (AD) (2017) 51. The learned Advocate lastly submits that there is no paper from the side of the Government-petitioner, showing that the property has become enlisted ever as enemy or vested property in the census list under the ambit of Defense of Pakistan Rules, 1965 and there is no gazette notification even from the side of the Government showing or treating that the property as vested or enemy property and the learned trial court as well as the appellate court after proper assessment of evidence and appreciation of law decided the merit of the suit in favour of the plaintiffs rightly and there is no misreading or non reading of evidence or non consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice by which the impugned judgment and decree can be interfered with. 

 10. Considering the submission of the learned Advocates, having gone through the judgment and decree passed by the trial court as well as the appellate court along with the evidence on records, both oral and documentary, it transpires that, admittedly the suit property appertaining to mouza Chandpur under Meherpur District originally belonged to one Gopi Dasi and the SA khatian No. 343 was correctly prepared in her name. It has been specifically contended from the side of the plaintiffs in their pleadings that the original owner of the property by a registered sub-kabala deed dated 4-2-1960 AD transferred the suit property along with her other property in favour of one Moyzuddin (vide Exhibit-1), who subsequently transferred the land by several sub-kabala deeds. It is also the pleading's case of the plaintiffs that the purchaser Moyzuddin after his purchase mutated his name in the Government Seresta and mutation khatian was opened in his name (vide Exhibit-2). It is further case of the plaintiffs that the subsequent purchasers from Mayzuddin after their purchase also mutated their names and paid rent to the Government and the Government after accepting rent from them granted rent receipts. The series of documentary evidences showing the tenancy of the plaintiffs predecessor and the plaintiffs including the Rent Receipts showing payment of rents to the Government has been proved under the law of Evidence (Act No. 1 of 1872), which has been marked as Exhibits-1 series, 2, 2(ka), 3, 3(ka), 4 & 5. Besides these, the plaintiffs in order to prove their case have adduced 3 witnesses and to substantiate the solenama which was filed by the plaintiffs and the defendant No. 2 Ruhul Amin, the plaintiff No. 1 and the defendant No. 2 deposed before the trial court. 

 16. In the foregoing narrative, it is apparent from the face of the papers that from the side of the defendant-petitioner during trial of the original suit no witness was examined to corroborate the case of the Government and with regard to this, in the case of Government of Bangladesh vs Md Mizanur Rahman 5 CLR (AD) 51 their Lordships held that, " if no witness examined and no statement made before the Court in relation to matters of fact under inquiry, that means, the facts stated in the plaint were not stated before the court on the date fixed for hearing of the suit and in fact, it is only the pleading of the plaintiff. 

 18. Furthermore, it has been proved by sufficient credible tangible evidence that prior to 1965 AD the property-in-dispute has been transferred by the admitted original owner of the suit property, and, as such, the property cannot be declared enemy property or vested property under the Defence of Pakistan Rules, 1965. In absence of any Government notification published in any official gazette as to the nature of the property as enemy property or vested property as alleged from the side of the Government, it cannot be held that the property, under the Purview of Defence of Pakistan Rules, 1965 has become vested or non resident property or that it has been leased out in favour of any body. 

 20. In the result; the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and decree dated 12-11-2008 and 18-11-2008 respectively passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Meherpur in Title Appeal No. 68 of 1999 affirming those of dated 24-2-1999 and 28-2-1999 respectively passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Meherpur Sadar, Meherpur in Title Suit No. 326 of 1995 is hereby affirmed.

parties:
Ratton Sarker and others ------ Defendant-Respondent-Petitioners
-Versus-
Rupak Bar and others ----- Plaintiff-Appellant-Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Mr. Soumendra Sarker, J. :- The Rule issued calling upon the opposite parties No.1-10 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 12.04.2012 passed by the learned District Judge, Barisal in Title Appeal No.102 of 2011 allowing the appeal reversing those of dated 15.06.2011 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st court, Barisal in Title Suit No.31 of 2009 dismissing the suit should not be set aside and/or pass such other order or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

 2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule in a nutshell can be stated thus, the present opposite parties No.1-10 as plaintiffs instituted the original Title Suit being No.31 of 2009 in the 1st Court of learned Joint District Judge, Barisal for declaration of title in the land described in schedule 'kas of the plaint contending inter cilia, that the suit property appertaining to Mouza-Bogra Alekanda under J.L. No.50 of Police. Station and District-Barisal, corresponding to R.S. khatian No.1417 and S.A. khatian No.1987, in plotNo.5216 consists of an area .11 acres and .02 acres in plot No.5239 in all .13 acres of land originally belonged to one Nibaran Chandra Bar. Nibaran Chandra Bar during his life time had been owning and possessing the suit property and subsequently transferred the suit land in favour of his two sons Dipok Bar and Dilip Bar and grandsons Mikel P.K. Bar, Pulak Bar and Rupak Bar by an unregistered deed of gift dated 20.04.1979 and handed over possession to them. Subsequently; Nibaran Chandra died on 20.09.1980. Among the aforesaid gift holders, on 10.08.1981 Dilip Bar, Mikel P.K. Bar and Rupak Bar transferred their portion of land in favour of Dipak Bar by a deed of gift. Thereafter; Dipak Bar by virtue of a Mutation Case being No.593/1981-82 mutated his name in the Government 'Serest-a' and paying rents regularly for the suit property. Subsequently; Dipak Bar mortgaged .51/2 acres of land in favour of Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation and in lieu of that; obtained loan from Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation. After taking loan keeping mortgage of some of the properties, Dipak Bar erected a semi-pakka dwelling house consists-of 03 bed rooms, kitchen and latrine therein and started to reside therein with his family members. Thereafter; Dipak Bar died leaving behind three sons namely the plaintiff No.1 Rupak Bar and the predecessor of the plaintiffs No.2-5 Mikel P.K. Bar and the predecessor of the plaintiff No.6 & 7 Pulak Bar with two daughters the plaintiff No.8 & 9 and one wife, the plaintiff No.10 and in this way the heirs of Dipak Bar use to reside in the suit homestead property after payment of the loan amount in favour of Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation. It is the case of the plaintiffs that the 'defendants having no manner of right, title, interest and possession in the suit property, on the basis of false allegation claimed the suit property on 22.04.2008 and tried to mutate their names at which the title of the plaintiffs have been clouded and to dispel that cloud, they have instituted the original suit. 

 3. The contrary case of the contesting defendants No.1, 2 and 4 in short is thus that the property-in-dispute originally belonged to Nibaran Chandra Bar and he died leaving behind his heirs two sons Dipak Bar and Dilip Bar with one daughter Era Bar and in this way the sons and daughter of the original owner became the owner of the suit property. After the death of Dilip Bar his one wife Saraj Bar and brother Dipak Bar and sister Era Bar became the owner and possessors of the suit property. The further case of the defendants is such that the wife of Dilip Bar died leaving behind three sons namely Mikel P.K. Bar, Pulak Bar and Rupak Bar with two daughters; the plaintiffs No.8 and 9. Subsequently, Pulak Bar died leaving behind his one daughter the plaintiff No.6 and one wife Jesika Bar and in this way the heirs and successive heirs of Dipak Bar used to possess the suit property. The plaintiffs No.1-5 with an ill-motive to deprive the defendants created two deed of gifts and in fact Nibaran Chandra Bar or Dilip Bar never executed any deed of gift as alleged from the side of the plaintiffs and as such the plaintiff's suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 4. The learned trial court during trial of the original suit after framing 05 (five) different issues decided the issues on maintainability, limitation and defect of party in favour of the plaintiffs and decided the issue on right, title, interest and possession, against the plaintiffs and thereby dismissed the suit on 15.06.2011. 

 8. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners submits that the learned appellate court during disposal of the appeal misdirected himself in his total approach of the matter and thereby committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate further submits that the learned District Judge, Barisal at the time of passing the impugned judgment and decree failed to appreciate the exact proposition of law and also failed to assess the evidence on record in its true perspective. The learned Advocate also submits that admittedly the property-in-dispute originally belonged to Nibaran Chandra Bar and it is the positive contention of the plaintiffs that, by two deeds of gift, they have acquired the suit property and possessing the same, but the plaintiffs to the suit have failed to prove that the executants of the deeds in fact executed the deeds in favour of the donees and there is no direct evidence of possession in favour of the plaintiffs. The learned Advocate argued that none of the plaintiff's witnesses have been able to prove the case of the plaintiffs and the P.Ws. are not competent, disinterested and trustworthy while the defendant's witnesses have successfully proved the case of the defendants and disproved the case of the plaintiffs, which is totally ignored by the learned appellate court. The learned Advocate lastly submits that the trial court during disposal of the original suit rightly under the ambit of Order V, rule 20 of the Code of Civil Procedure after proper evaluation of the evidence on records dismissed the suit on contest. But the learned appellate court without reversing the findings of the trial court reversed the judgment and decree of the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Barisal and as such the impugned judgment and decree is not sustainable in law and facts. 

 9. As against the aforesaid submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioners, the learned advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite parties opposing the Rule controverted the argument advanced from the side of the petitioners and submits that the learned appellate court during disposal of the appeal committed no illegality or irregularity. The learned Advocate further submits that the plaintiffs to the suit by adducing sufficient tangible, credible evidence both oral and documentary have successfully proved that they have acquired their valid right, title, interest and possession in the suit property by virtue of their deeds of gift and as successors of the original admitted owner Nibaran Chandra Bar and that the plaintiffs to the suit after acquiring the suit property possessing the same after mutating their names in the government `seresta' and by regular payment of rents to the government. The learned Advocate also submits that the trial court during disposal of the original suit decided in his judgment and decree that the suit in its present form is maintainable and there is no legal bar of institution of the original suit and the learned Joint District Judge, 1' Court, Barisal also decided conclusively that the suit is not barred by limitation and bad for defect of parties. The only point for dismissal the suit was such by the learned trial court that the title and interest of the suit property is not proved from the side of the plaintiffs. The learned Advocate argued that against the observation and decisions of the trial court on point of limitation, defect of party and maintainability, the defendants did not file any appeal or cross-objection and thereby it is the proposition of law that they have admitted that findings and decisions of the trial court which is apparently against them. The leaned Advocate submits that the deeds of gift as contended from the side of the plaintiffs in their pleading, has been duly proved and those were exhibited under the provisions of Evidence Act without any objection. The learned Advocate lastly submits that in the year 1979 there was no provision that the unregistered deed of gift is not valid in the eye of law and the learned trial court is totally misconceived in holding the view that the title documents of the plaintiffs are not proved. The learned Advocate in his submissions categorically pointed out the evidence on records and submits that the learned appellate court at the time of deciding the merit of the appeal rightly after proper sifting of evidence and assessment of the same in its true perspective on proper appreciation of law decided the merit of the suit in favour of the plaintiffs and rebutted the findings of the trial court, adverting evidence on records and thereafter; reversed the findings and judgment passed by the trial court and in the impugned judgment and decree there is no misreading or non-reading of evidence or non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice, by which the impugned judgment and decree can be interfered with. 

 10. In order to appreciate the submission of the learned counsels, having gone through the respective cases of the parties and the judgment and decree passed by the learned trial court as well as the appellate court in consultation with the evidence on records and the pleadings of the parties it transpires that the suit property appertaining to Mouza Bogra Alekanda under Barisal Sadar Upazila corresponding to R.S. khatian No.1417 and S.A. Khatian No.1987 in plot No.5216 of the S.A. khatian No.1987 consists of an area 0.11 acres and .02 acres of S.A. plot No.5239 in all .13 acres of land originally belonged to one Nibaran Chandra Bar. Nibaran Chandra Bar during his life time had been owning and possessing the suit property and thereafter transferred the suit land in favour of his two sons Dipok Bar and Dilip Bar and grandsons Mikel P.K. Bar, Pulak Bar and Rupak Bar by an unregistered deed of gift dated 20.04.1979, which was written on 19.04.1979. It was further contention of the plaintiffs that the admitted owner of the property after execution of the deed of gift handed over possession of the suit property in favour of the aforesaid 05 donees. Subsequently; by another deed of gift dated 10.08.1981 Mikel P.K. Bar, Pulok Bar and Rupak Bar transferred their share in favour of Dipak Bar. The aforesaid two deeds of gift have been marked as Exhibit-7 and 7(ka) after its formal proof. by the attesting witness of the deeds P.W.2 Pal Sarnendu Sarker, who in fact proved the deeds dated 20.04.1979 and 10.08.1981. It further transpires from the papers on records that the plaintiffs in order to prove their case have produced the R.S. khatian No.1417 and S.A. Khatian No.1987 which has been marked as Exhibit No.2 and 3 respectively. Besides this; the Mutation Khatian No.16008 and the paper relating to Mutation Case No.593KT/81-82 has also been produced from the side of the plaintiffs in respect of the suit land and these papers have been marked as Exhibit-4 and 5 respectively by which the plaintiff Dipak Bar have mutated his name in the government `seresia. The subsequent payment of rents in respect of the suit property followed by rent receipts were also produced from the side of the plaintiffs to substantiate their case. With regard to taking loan from Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation by Dipak Bar, the mortgage papers in respect of .5Y2 acres of land has been marked as Exhibit-2 by the trial court and it is the positive case of the plaintiffs in their pleadings that after taking loan, their predecessor have erected a semi-pacca dwelling house in the suit property and started to reside therein. The plaintiff's predecessor Dipak Bar opened a separate khatian in the government `seresta' and after payment of rent obtained rent receipt which is Exhibit-1. 

 13. P.W.1 is the plaintiff No.9 who is the daughter of Dipak Bar namely Orpa Bar. This witness deposed on behalf of all the plaintiffs. In her testimony, she has categorically testified that her grandfather Nibaron Chandra Bar was the original owner of the suit property and his grandfather gifted the property in favour of his sons Dipak Bar, Dilip Bar and three grand sons. In the said deed of gift of 20.04.1979 the witnesses were the Secretary of Baptist Church namely Smith Biswas and the President/Proctor of YMCA. P.W.1 further testified in her deposition that Dilip Bar subsequently by another deed of gift dated 10.08.1981 transferred his share in favour of his brother Dipok Bar. On the same date the 03 donees of the earlier gift deed, Mike! P.K. Bar, Pulak Bar and Rupak Bar transferred their share in favour of Dipak Bar and Dipak Bar in a mutation proceedings mutated his name and opened a separate khatian. He also paid rent for the suit property. The plaintiff No.9 to substantiate the pleadings of the plaintiffs also testified that her father Dipak Bar after taking loan from Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation erected a dwelling house consists of 03 rooms and used to reside therein with his family members. 

 20. On anxious consideration and assessment of mine on the evidence as adduced from the sides of the respective parties, I find that the learned appellate court in his observation and findings categorically adverting evidence on records reversed the findings of the trial court as to the right, title, interest and possession of the parties and after proper evaluation of the evidences, both oral and documentary, arrived at a conclusive decision that the plaintiffs to the suit have successfully discharged their onus in proving their respective case and there is no cogent and trustworthy evidence, which can be relied on from the side of the defendants to falsify the case of the plaintiffs. Under the ambit of Order XLI Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the learned appellate court elaborately discussed the evidence on records in its true perspective and thereafter decided the merit of the appeal in favour of the plaintiff-appellants therein. There is no misreading or non-reading of evidence or non-consideration of material facts, resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice, by which it can be held that the impugned judgment and decree suffers from any sort of illegality or infirmity. Relying upon two decisions reported in 29 DLR 239 and 2 ADC 211, the learned District Judge, Barisal rightly decided the points in hands and the matter of adverse possession and hence, I find no ambiguity or misquoting of the provision of law as alleged from the side of the present petitioners, in the impugned judgment and decree. As to the acquisition of the right, title, interest and possession in the suit property the evidence adduced from the side of the plaintiffs led me to draw such inference that in the suit property the plaintiffs have acquired a valid right, title, interest and they are possessing the same. 

 21. It is to be remembered that, under section 49 of the Registration Act [XVI of 1908], a document which is required to be registered under this Act, but not registered, yet be admitted for collateral purposes, as to prove the nature of possession and such an ancient document can be used to prove acquisition of title by adverse possession in appropriate cases. 

 23. In the result, the Rule is discharged. The impugned judgment and decree dated 12.04.2012 passed by the learned District Judge, Barisal in Title Appeal No.102 of 2011 allowing the appeal reversing those of dated 15.06.2011 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1 st court, Barisal in Title Suit No.31 of 2009 dismissing the suit is hereby affirmed.
