learned District Judge, Thakurgaon in Civil Revision No.7 of 2010 affirming the judgment and order dated 09.03.2010 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Haripur, Thakurgaon in Title Suit No.70 of 2008 should not be set aside and / or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem lit and proper. 

 2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule in a nutshell can he stated thus the present opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff instituted the original Title Suit No.82 of 2004 in the Court of learned Assistant Judge, Thakurgaon which was subsequently transferred to the Court of learned Assistant Judge. Haripur Thakurgaon and renumbered as Title Suit No.70 of 2008. The present petitioner as defendant No.10 contested the suit by filing written statement. When the suit was pending for hearing before the trial Court the present petitioner on the ground of his illness submitted adjournment prayer. Thereafter the suit was fixed on 09.03.2010 for further preemptory hearing which was cross-examination of the witnesses of the defendant Nos.I-2 and 5. The present defendant-petitioner on that date prayed time for further hearing on the ground of his sudden pain in chest supported by Medical certificate and the plaintiff made his appearance in the form of filing iliajira'. The defendants witnesses did not file 'hajira' and remain absent. The learned Assistant Judge rejected the defendant's prayer for time and fixed a date for hearing argument. 

 7. As against the aforesaid submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party No.1 opposing the Rule controverted the arguments advanced from the side of the petitioner and submits that the learned trial Court as well as the I" revisional Court committed no illegality or irregularity in rejecting the time petition and thereafter in disallowing the Civil Revision being No.7 of 2010. The learned Advocate further submits that the defendant-petitioner during pre-emptory hearing of the original suit obtained as many as 24 (twenty four) adjournments which is unwarranted in law. Under the 

 8. Heard the teamed Advocates of both sides. perused the impugned judgment and order 4 along with the order of rejection of rime prayer passed by the trial Court on 09.03.2010 in Title Suit No.70 of 2008. I have also perused the order sheets marked Annexure-"C" and the adjournment prayer of the defendant-petitioner marked as Annexure-A. 

 9. On perusal of the connected papers it transpires that the original suit was fixed for further pre-emptory (F.P.H.) hearing on 09.03.2010 and on that date the defendant No.10 filed an application for adjournment supported by a Medical certificate. The date was fixed for cross-examination of the witnesses adduced from the side of the defendant Nos. -2 and 5. It further appears that the defendant-petitioner after getting summon-notice made his appearance and submitted written statement. From the observation of the 1" revisional Court it is noticed that the defendant-petitioner from his appearance dated 28.11.2006 till 09.03.2010 obtained about three years time after filing several applications. The 1st  revisional Court consulting the order sheet of the original case record inserted 24 dates of adjournments taken by the defendant petitioner and obviously decided the merit of the revisional application in favour of the plaintiff-opposite party therein. 

 12. In the result, the Rule having no merit is discharged without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and order dated 10.07.2011 passed by the learned District Judge, Thakurgaon in Civil Revision No.7 of 2010, affirming the judgment and order dated 09.03.2010 passed by the leaned Assistant Judge, Haripur, Thakurgaon in Title Stilt No.70 of 2008 is hereby affirmed.

parties:
Amir Hossain Mallick
Vs.
Ali Hossain Mridha and others
full_judgment:
Soumendra Sarker, J: The Rule issued calling upon the Opposite Party Nos.1-14 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 03.06.1998 and 20.09.1998 respectively passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Court, Barisal in Title Appeal No.42 of 1996 affirming the judgment and decree dated 31.01.1996 and 06.02.1996 respectively passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Barisal in Title Suit No.91 of 1994 should not be set aside and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper. 

 2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule in a nutshell can be stated thus, the present petitioner as plaintiff instituted the original Title Suit No.91 of 1994 in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Barisal against the present opposite-party Nos. 1-3/11-20 and one Chand Baru bibi, the predecessor opposite party Nos. 4-10 for declaration of title in the land described in schedule "ka" of the plaint and for declaration that the auction sale mentioned in schedule "Kha" of the plaint is collusive, fraudulent and false with a further declaration that the V.P. proceedings described in schedule "Ga" of the plaint is illegal, without jurisdiction and not binding upon the plaintiff contending inter-alia that the suit property originally belonged to one Jogendra Nath who purchased the same in the benami of one Mathura Nath and Sukumar out of his own money. The R.S. record was prepared in the name of Mathura Nath. Subsiquently, Jogendra Nath executed a will in favour of one Shachindra Nath in the year 1356 B.S. and thereafter Jogendra Nath died on 14.04.1960 A.D. Shachindra Nath filed a Probate case being No.32 of 1960 in which Probate was granted on 11.01.1962. Subsequently while Mathura Nath and Sukumar challenged the execution of will and also denied to execute a deed of nadabi in favour of Shachindra Nath a Title Suit being No. 97/98 of 1963 was filed by Shachindra Nath. That suit was decreed in favour of Shachindra. Thereafter Shachindra mutated his name in S.A. khatian No. 210. Shachindra Nath transferred the suit property in favour of the defendant Nos.9-11 who sold out the same in favour of the plaintiff on 25.02.1964. Subsequently the plaintiff mutated his name and paid rent to the Government. The plaintiff came to know that the suit land was auction sold in favour of the defendant Nos.1-5 on 29.05.1955 in a Rent Suit No. 91 of 1954 and by virtue of a Execution Case No. 339 of 1955 auction purchasers mutated their names in the S.A. khatian for the suit land. The Rent Suit was false, collusive and created. The further case of the plaintiff is such that the original owner of the land was all along a citizen of this country and he never migrated to India and as such the suit land cannot be a vested property. The plaintiff in the 1st part of Chaitra, 1396 B.S. came to learn about the vested property proceeding as well as the auction purchase of the defendant Nos.1-5 and thereafter he filed the original suit against the defendants. 

 3. The contrary case of the contesting defendant No.6 in short is such that one Kalma Jamindari Company Ltd was the superior landlord of the suit property. After the acquisition of Jamindari estate by the Government the superior landlord exhausted his interest and right, title over the disputed property and taking compensation money he surrendered the property in favour of the Government and the Government since then possessing the land as khash land under the Government. That .49 acres of land has been declared vested property rightly and the Government granted lease for that portion of land and the lessee is possessing the same. The plaintiff having no manner of right, title, interest and possession in the disputed properly on the basis of some forged created papers filed the suit on false allegation which is liable to be dismissed. 

 4. The learned trial court after taking evidence dismissed the suit on contest by its judgment and decree dated 31.01.1996 in Title Suit No. 91 of 1994. 

 8. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits that the learned courts below during disposal of the original suit and its subsequent appeal committed illegality in not considering the plaint case and the evidence adduced from the side of the plaintiff-petitioner. The learned Advocate during his argument pressed paragraph No. 8 of the revisional application wherein it is stated that the plaintiff-petitioner in his plaint and evidence stated that Shachindra Nath, the predecessor of the plaintiff filed Title Suit No.97 of 1962 for declaration of title and confirmation of possession against Mathura Das and others. That suit was decreed ex-parte on 22.12.1962 but the certified copy of the aforesaid decree was not filed in the trial court. On 01.10.1996 the plaintiff-appellant-petitioner accordingly filed the application along with a certified copy of the aforesaid decree under order 41 rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure and at the time of hearing of the appeal the appellant prayed for marking the certified copy of the decree as exhibit but the learned lower appellate court did not consider the application and marked the paper as exhibit which is an error on the face of the record and that has resulted serious miscarriage of justice. The learned Advocate lastly submits that the plaintiff-appellant-petitioner to prove his case prays for an order of remand so that he can able to prove his case and falsified the case of the defendants. 

 9. As against the aforesaid submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party opposing the Rule controverted the submissions advanced from the side of the petitioner and submits that the trial court as well as appellate court during disposal of the original suit and its subsequent appeal committed no illegality or irregularity. There is no misreading or non-reading of evidence and non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in deciding the merit of the appeal against the appellant and in favour of the respondent and there is nothing to interfere with the impugned judgment and decree passed by the lower appellate court which is the final court of facts. The learned Advocate further submits that the plaintiff-appellant-petitioner filed the application under order 41 Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 01.10.1996 A.D. before the appellate court and the appellate court hearing the parties to the case passed his judgment on 20.09.1998. By this time from 01.10.1996 to 20.09.1998 the plaintiff-appellant remained dormant and took no step for hearing and disposal of that application. The teamed Advocate also submits that the contents of the application is not consistent with the plaint of the plaintiff and in the plaint along with the appeal-memo the plaintiff-appellant did not state the actual number and year of the Civil Suit allegedly instituted by Shachindra Nath. Even the date of its decree was not cited therein. The content of the application under order 41 Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure is vague upon which no concrete decision can be taken and as such the learned lower appellate court did not pass any order for the aforesaid ambiguity. The learned Advocate lastly submits that the plaintiff's plaint does not disclose any definite cause of action as in paragraph No. 11 of the plaint there is no insertion of month of alleged cause of action of the plaintiff for which the plaintiff allegedly constrained to institute the original suit. 

 12. Having gone through the original plaint of the plaintiff-petitioner 1 find that in his pleadings there is a recital of the plaintiff that while Mathura Nath and Sukumar Das denied to execute “না-দাবী মুক্তি পত্র” in favour of Shachindra Nath, Shachindra Nath filed a Title Suit in the 3rd court of the then Suboidinate Judge, Barisal being Title Suit No.97/98 of 1963 and obtained decree therein. It is to be noticed here that the aforesaid decree is the basis of plaintiff’s case. In consultation with the application under order 41 Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure there is a glaring discrepancy which is the number of Title Suit as cited by the plaintiff-petitioner in the said application and that Title Suit is 97 of 1962. Apart from this; I have come-across from the pleadings of the plaintiff that the plaintiff failed to state the month in which his cause of auction was allegedly accrued. In this context; it is needless to advert that the contention of the plaintiff-petitioner apparently suffers from material contradiction and omission which cannot be ignored. The submissions advanced from the side of the learned Advocate for the opposite-party have got every nexus with the case records. The learned courts below in deciding the fate of the suit and its subsequent appeal rightly held that the plaintiff to the suit since not able to prove his case he is not entitled to get any relief as prayed for. The assessment of evidence as it appears within the findings of the lower appellate court appears to be fair and legal and no such misreading or non-reading of evidence and non-consideration of material fact is noticed by which it can be held that the impugned judgment and decree suffers from any sort of infirmity and illegality. Before departing with the case I like to advert that to fill up the lacuna there lies no scope to allow the application under order XLI, Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 14. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The judgment and decree dated 03.06.1998 and 20.09.1998 respectively passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Barisal in Title Appeal No.42 of 1996 affirming the judgment and decree dated 31.01.1996 and 06.02.1996 respectively passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Barisal in Title Suit No.91 of 1994 is hereby affirmed.

full_judgment:
The Leave was granted to decide as to whether the impugned order dated 18-10-2009 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 8th Court, Dhaka in Civil Revision No. 242 of 2009 reversing those of dated 19-7-2009 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 323 of 1999 is illegal. 

 2. The facts leading to the issuance to the leave in a nutshell; can be stated thus, the plaintiff-petitioner filed the original Title suit alleging that the plaintiff as a landlord on the basis of a written agreement dated 14th June, 1993 entered into a settlement with the Defendant-opposite- party which a voluntary organization namely Mukti Lawrence Foundation represented by it's Chairman to let out the schedule premises to the defendant foundation for a period of 5(five) years from 1-7-1993 to 30-6-1998 at a monthly rental of Taka 50,000 (fifty thousand) payable in favour of the landlord by the first week of the following month according to English calendar year. According to clause 3 (three) of the said agreement the defendant was required to pay 1(one) year's monthly rent in advance and accordingly the defendant paid Taka 6,00,000 (six lacs) to the attorney of the plaintiff through cheque. Subsequently the defendant since not paid rent from January, 1994 AD the plaintiff filed the original suit for eviction of the defendant from the suit premises. 

 3. The contrary case of the defendant No.1 is such, that the defendant is not a monthly tenant under the plaintiff. The defendant No.2 executed 'Bainanama' (Deed of agreement) and paid Taka 50,00000 (fifty lakh) out of the total consideration of Taka 90,00000 (ninety lakh) in respect of the disputed premises but the plaintiff violating the terms and conditions of the deed of agreement refused to make the deed registered in favour of the defendants and thereafter, the defendant filed a suit for specific performance of contract against the plaintiff being Other Class Suit No. 115 of 1997. In that suit the defendant who is the petitioner of Civil Revision No. 242 of 2009 after filing a written statement denied the case of the plaintiff therein but the plaintiff managed to obtain an exparte decree. Subsequent to that, the exparte decree was set-aside and the original suit was restored to its file and number. The petitioner who was the defendant No.2 of the suit then filed an application under Order VI, Rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure for furnishing further and better statement. 

 4. The learned trial Court in Title Suit No. 323 of 1999 vide his order dated 19-7-2009 rejected the prayer for furnishing further and better statement and fixed a date for pre-emptory hearing of the original suit. 

 5. Being aggrieved the defendant preferred Civil Revision No. 242 of 2009 in the Court of learned District Judge, Dhaka which was heard and disposed of by the learned Additional District Judge, 8th Court, Dhaka and the learned first Revisional Court by the impugned judgment and order dated 18-10-2009 allowed the Civil Revision reversing the judgment and order of the trial Court passed in Title Suit No. 323 of 1999. 

 9. As against the aforesaid submissions of the learned counsel for the petitioner the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite-party controverting the grounds of the Revisional application submits that the learned first revisional Court in passing the impugned judgment and order committed no illegality or irregularity or non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice by which it can be held that the impugned judgment and order is perverse and not sustainable in law. The learned Advocate further submits that the plaintiff despite was not the owner of the suit premises entered into a collusive forged agreement deed with the defendant and it was not within the knowledge of the defendant at the time of filing the original written statement. Subsequently while the matter has come into the notice of the defendant he filed an application under Order VI, rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure for furnishing further and better statement in as much as it was very much applicable as well as acceptable for proper adjudication into the matter in dispute. The learned Advocate for the opposite-party also submits that by further and better statement their original pleadings in the written statement as submitted earlier from the side of the defendant No. 2 is not contradicted or denied substantially. By the subsequent factual aspect the defendant wants to get a chance to bring it into the notice of the Court that a fraud has been practiced by the plaintiff with him and he was not in the know ledge at the time of entering into the contract with the plaintiff in respect of the suit premises. The learned Advocate lastly submits that the plaintiff to the suit if the further & better statement is accepted has nothing to lose rather he has sufficient scope to controvert the pleadings of the defendant by adducing oral and documentary evidence (if any), but if the defendant is deprived from furnishing better particulars in the form of better statement there would be multiplicity of suit and there is no law forbidding the defendant to amend his pleadings to establish his positive case. 

 10. Heard the learned Advocates of both sides, perused the case record, impugned judgment and order along with the order passed by the learned trial Court i.e. the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka dated 19-7-2009 in Title Suit No. 323 of 1999. 

 11. On perusal of the connected papers it transpires that the defendant No.2 during pendency of the original suit under the ambit of Order VI, Rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure submitted further and better statement alleging that the plaintiff-opposite-party-petitioner Dr AH Md. Ali Haider Qureshi filed a Title Suit being No. 578 of 1979 in the 4th Court of learned Joint District Judge, Dhaka claiming that he is the ‘বেনামদার’ of his wife which was subsequently renumbered as Title Suit No. 18 of 1985 in the 1st Court of learned Joint District Judge, Dhaka and the learned Court decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff. Subsequently; that decree was set-aside by this Court and ultimately the. Hon'ble Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh affirmed the judgment and order and set-aside the judgment of the trial Court. By furnishing further and better statement the defendant No.2 wants to bring it into the notice of the Court that the plaintiff is no longer the owner of the disputed premises rather his wife Dr. Shahin Qureshi is the actual owner. The learned trial Court vide his order dated 19-7-2009 rejected the said further and better statement of the defendant No. 2 and the defendant No. 2 subsequent to that filed the Civil Revision No. 242 of 2009. The learned first revisional Court i.e. the Additional District Judge, 8th Court, Dhaka by the impugned judgment and order opined that the defendant No.2 in his further and better statement (Annexure-C) clearly states about his specific case and by stating the reason for which the ownership of the plaintiff in the disputed premises has been seized and reason for which the suit for specific performance of contract was not conducted. It was also narrated by the defendant No. 2 in his further and better statement that as to why he has stopped in paying rent to the plaintiff for the disputed premises; which has elucidated the pleadings of the defendant. The learned first revisional Court in his observation citing the Provisions laid down in Order VI, Rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure observed that by further and better statement the original pleadings of the defendant not contradicted and as because the matter was not known to the defendant earlier he could not furnish the respective factual aspect in his earlier written statement. 

 13. Having regard to the above mentioned decisions I do admit that under the provisions laid down in section 116 of the Evidence Act by the principle of estoppel in an appropriate case a ten- ant is stopped from furnishing better particulars. In our instant case as we have come across that during the continuance of the original suit i.e. during pendency of the suit before the trial Court it has come to the notice of the defendant No.2 that the plaintiff is not the owner of the suit premises and by practicing fraud with the defendant he entered into an agreement with him in respect of the premises in which he has no manner of tenancy right. As soon as it has come to his notice he submits further and better statement narrating the factual aspect supported by adequate papers. The learned first revisional Court during disposal of the Civil Revision being No. 242 of 2009 rightly held that the pleadings of the party not contradicted rather by furnishing further and better particulars the actual facts prevailing has brought into the notice of the Court and the plaintiff to the suit have every opportunity to falsify the plea of the defendant as alleged therein during trial of the original suit after adducing tangible, cogent and credible evidence. 

 17. The impugned judgment and order dated 18-10-2009 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 8th Court, Dhaka in Civil Revision No. 242 of 2009 reversing those of dated 19-7- 2009 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 323 of 1999 is hereby affirmed.

full_judgment:
2. Relevant facts, in short, are that the opposite party No.1, Sonali Bank as plaintiff instituted a suit being Title Suit No.44 of 1991 on 11-3-1991 before the Artha Rin Adalat, Dhaka praying for realisation of Taka 5,47,51,652 from the defendant-opposite party Nos.2-8 by selling the mortgaged property. The opposite party Nos. 2-6 and 7 as defendant Nos.1, 4 and 5 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement denying most of the allegations of the plaint. The present petitioner, Bangladesh Shilpa Bank Ltd. was defendant No. 7, who also contested the suit by filing a written statement. 

 3. The Artha Rin Adalat upon examining the pleadings of the parties framed necessary issues and then took evidence of both the sides and by the impugned judgment and decree dated 21-5-1996 decreed the suit in preliminary form on contest against the defendant Nos. 2, 3 and 6 with cost and dismissed the suit on contest against the defendant No. 7, Bangladesh Shilpa Bank Ltd as well as ex-parte against defendant No. 8, Sheikh Akizuddin Limited without cost. Subsequently, the preliminary decree for sale was drawn up on 11-7-1996 and as the defendants against whom the suit was decreed failed to pay the decreetal amount within the statutory period, the preliminary decree dated 11-7-1996 was made final on 8-10-1996. Thereafter, the decree-holder-Bank put the decree in execution being Title Execution Case No. 137 of 1997 on 17-6-1997 against the present opposite party Nos. 2-8 for realization of Taka 16,99,39,286.75 as calculated up to 31-5-1997. Subsequently, in the said execution case, the schedule property of opposite party Nos. 2-8 Company, which was mortgaged with Bangladesh Shilpa Bank Ltd was put to auction sale fixing on 12-3-1981. Challenging the said order of auction sale the petitioner, Bangladesh Shilpa Bank Ltd filed an application under Order XXI, rule 69 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for stoppage of the auction sale. The learned Subordinate Judge and the Artha Rin Adalat being executing Court rejected the said application on 14-1-2001 against which the present petitioner, Bangladesh Shilpa Bank Ltd filed Civil Revision No. 2254 of 2001 on 7-1-2001 before this Court. 

 7. On the other hand, Mr M Khaled Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 supports the impugned judgment and order, which was according to him, just correct and proper. He next relying on a number of decisions namely the decisions reported in 53 DLR (AD) 12, 24 BLD (AD) 223, 47 DLR (AD) 1, 13 BLD (AD) 56, 11 BLD 312 and an unreported judgment dated 4-3-2008 passed in Writ Petition No. 5673 of 2005 submits that in a frivolous case or misconceived suit the Court below is competent to entertain an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of miscellaneous case or any proceeding. He then submits that Order XXI, rule 58 of the Code of Civil Procedure provided remedy for third party but in this case admittedly, Bangladesh Shilpa Bank Ltd as defendant No. 7 contested the original Title suit No. 44 of 1991 and therefore, Miscellaneous Case No. 28 of 2001 as filed the petitioner Bangladesh Shilpa Bank Ltd was apparently misconceived and incompetent one.

parties:
GSH Jamal ----- Defendant-Appellant
vs
Surraiya Jabeen and ors ----- Plaintiff-Respondents
full_judgment:
Mirza Hussain Haider  J: This appeal is directed against the judgment and decree dated 23-9- 2008, passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 40 of 2005 (Originally Title Suit No. 135 of2003) decreeing the suit in favour of the plaintiff-landlord, holding that the defendant tenant is a defaulter and, as such, he is liable to be evicted and was also directed the defendant-tenant to vacate the suit premises upon removing all the structures constructed by him from the suit premises and handover the vacant possession of the same to the plaintiff landlord within 30 days. 

 3. By amending the plaint it has been alleged that the defendant in violation of the terms of the agreement constructed Semi Pucca structures in the vacant Space, Unauthorizedly, and thereby the residential nature of the suit premises has been converted into commercial and, as such, the tenant is liable to be evicted from the suit premises upon removing the unauthorized constructions at his own cost for violation of the terms of agreement as provided in the terms of the said agreement. It is further contended that the tenant obtained order from the House Rent Controller in House Rent Case No. 12 of 1997 to deposit Taka 53,200 per month which is contrary to the agreement dated 22-1-1995 and, as such, the plaintiff preferred an appeal against the said order of the Rent Controller which is pending. It is alleged further that the defendant tenant did not pay the entire amount of rent as per agreement which is Taka 2,000 per day i.e. Taka 60,000 per month in the House Rent Controller. Thus apart from being a defaulter he is also liable to be evicted for violating the terms of agreement as provided under section 18 of the premises Rent Control Act, 1991. It is further alleged that the defendant tenant filed Title Suit No.38 of 1991 subsequently, remembered as TitleSuit No.157 of 1999 in the 3rd Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka against the plaintiff landlords, wherein he prayed for temporary injunction for restraining the landlords from evicting the tenant from the suit premises. Such conduct of the defendant, it is alleged, shows that he does not want to vacant the suit premises rather possessing the same illegally on different pretexts, Hence the suit. 

 4. The defendant tenant contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material allegations of the plaint contending inter alia that since long before, the predecessor of the defendant tenant having good relationship with the predecessor of the plaintiffs entered into two agreements for monthly tenancy of the suit premises on 12-1-1988; The rents were paid regularly. Thereafter the agreement being renewed from time to time after every two years the defendant tenant, is running the business of "Shapla Community Centre" in the suit premises; After the demise of both the original land lord and the original tenant the agreements were entered into and renewed from time to time between the present plaintiffs and the present defendant. For renovation of the community centre the defendant tenant spent Taka 75,00,000 and the tenant having paid rent regularly to the landlord within time he is not a defaulter. Pursuant to the good relationship between the families the tenant did not keep with him all the renewed agreements and the copy of all the rent receipt; after expiry of the lease deeds in question on 31-12-1996 the agreements were renewed pursuant to the discussions between them for the year 1997- 1998 and the defendant tenant, pursuant to such agreement as well as the discussions continued his business of running community centre in the suit premises. But when the landlord did not adjust the rent for the month of December 1995 with the security money, kept in deposit with them, the defendant tenant paid the rent of the said month on 8-12-1996. Subsequently, having failed to get the agreement renewed on requests the defendant tenant a legal notice upon the plaintiff landlords on 26-12-1996 through his Advocate and the plaintiff landlords having received the said notice did not reply to the same, as such another legal notice was issued by the defendant, which returned undelivered. However, the defendant tenant continued paying rent up to December 1996 which the landlord received upon issuing rent receipts. But however, when the defendant tenant wanted to pay rent for the month of January 1997, the plaintiff landlords refused to receive the same with intention to make the defendant tenant a defaulter. Understanding the said intention of the landlords, the tenant, on 8-1-1997 sent Taka 52,000 by Money Order to the plaintiff landlords which the plaintiffs, on 15-1-1997 refused to accept and the said refused having been received on 21-1-1997 by the tenant, House Rent Case No. 12 of 1997 was filed before the House Rent Controller for depositing the rent and since then the tenant had been depositing the rent regularly in accordance with law. The House Rent Controller by his order dated 17-1-2000 allowed the case of the defendant tenant and directed him to deposit Taka 53,200 as rent with the House Rent Controller regularly. It is further contended by the defendant tenant that he was compelled to file Title Suit No. 34 of 1997 (subsequently renumbered as Title Suit No. 157 of 1999 of the 3rd Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka) and obtained an ad interim order of injunction therein which is still pending. Thus the tenant is not a defaulter in the eye of law and he is running his business in the suit premises ad earning his livelihood through the said business. In case the defendant is evicted from the suit premises he will be in grave trouble as such the suit should be dismissed. 

 5. Considering the pleading of both the parties, the learned Joint District Judge framed as many as seven issues including the issue as to whether the defendant having not paid rent is a defaulter, whether the defendant constructed any unauthorized structures and running the business of Shapla Community Center; whether pursuant to the agreement the defendant tenant is liable to pay Taka 2000 as compensation on the expiry of the agreement, whether the tenant is liable to be evicted for violating the terms of the agreement; whether the plaintiff is entitled to get relief as prayed for on evicting the defendant tenant upon removing the unauthorized structures thereon' and recovery of arrear rent including compensation. 

 6. The plaintiffs in support of their claim adduced two witnesses including plaintiff No.3 (a) as PW 1 and the learned Advocate who issued the legal notice as PW 2. On the other hand, the defendant tenant adduced himself only as DW 1. The plaintiff landlords in support of their case made out in the plaint filed four exhibits including two agreements in question dated 22-1-1995 (Exhibit X, XI = 4, 4(ka), the legal notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act (Exhibit 2 series) along with notice of RAJUK and the Works Department addressed top the plaintiff (Exhibit 3 to 3 (gha). On the other hand, the defendant tenant filed three Exhibits namely the judgment of the House Rent Control Case No. 12 of 1997 passed on 17-1-2000 (Exhibit "Ka"), order No.9 dated 9-6-1997 passed by in Title Suit No. 34 of 1997 subsequently re-numbered as Title Suit No. 157 of 1999 showing granting of injunction against the plaintiff landlords (Exhibit "Ka") and the legal notice dated 30-7-2003 issued by Mr Md Nurul Islam, Advocate on behalf of the plaintiff landlords upon the defendant tenant along with the registered receipt with AID (Exhibit "Ga", which has also been marked as Exhibit 2 series). 

 7. Upon considering the pleadings and the evidences on record, both oral and documentary, the learned Jude held that the suit is maintainable, the same is not barred by limitation, the defendant tenant as DW 1 having admitted that the rent for the month of December was paid on 8-12-1996, which is beyond the time fixed in the agreement and the rent for the month of January 1997 having paid on 25-1-1997 and the rent for the month of August 2003 having not at all being paid till date he has become a defaulter. Apart from this, upon examining the payment receipts as appears in the record of House Rent Control case No. 12 of 1997 the Court further held that the defendant tenant did not pay rent for the month of January 1997, February 1998, August 1998, December 1999, February 2001 within the stipulated period of first week of the month, as contemplated in the agreement, as such he has become a defaulter. It is further held that in violation of the terms of the agreements dated 22-1-1995 the defendant tenant constructed unauthorized structures and had been running the business of "Shapla Community Centre"; and the defendant tenant, pursuant to two agreements dated 22-1-1995 is liable to pay Taka 2000 as compensation, for each day's overstay in the suit premises after 31-12-1996; the Court also found that since the defendant tenant violated the terms of the agreement as such he is liable to be evicted. Accordingly the tenant defendant having not vacated the suit premises after the expiry of the agreement, he is liable to be evicted upon removing the unauthorized structures constructed therein with compensation and the plaintiff is entitled to get the arrear rents from the defendant for the period of his stay in the suit premises after 31-12-1996. With all these findings the learned Judge decreed the suit and directed the defendant to vacate the suit premises with 30 days upon removing the unauthorized structures situated thereon and also directed the defendant tenant to pay Taka 2000 per day i.e. Taka 60,000 per month and upon deducting Taka 53,200, which is being deposited with the Rent Controller, every month, from the said amount of Taka 60,000 the Court held that the remaining amount of Taka 6,800 is required to be paid from the date of expiry of the agreement till August 2008 i.e. 140 months which amounts to Taka 9,52,000 as compensation. The Court further deducted the security amount of Taka 2,08,000 from the said amount of Taka 9,52,000 and accordingly directed the defendant tenant to pay Taka 7,44,000 to the plaintiffs land lords. The defendant tenant has further been directed to pay the utility bills for the use of Electricity, WASA, GAS, Sewerage, telephone, etc, from 22-1-1995 till August 2008 and hand over the paid receipts to the plaintiff landlords in default the plaintiff be entitled to get the decree executed through Court. Hence this appeal. 

 8. Mr Mahbubey Alam, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant appellant (tenant) at the very outset admitted that the question for determination in this appeal is whether the appellant is a defaulter as defined under the provision of the Premises Rent Control Act and/or he is entitled to get protection under the said Act. In this respect he submits that after the determination of the tenancy when the tenant remains in possession he becomes a "statutory tenant" as such he cannot be evicted as a default if such tenant continues paying rent regularly within the stipulated time of 15 days of the month following as provided in the statute. Relying on the case of Maria Keshi D' Rozaria vs Hassan Movies Ltd, reported in 41 DLR (AD) 35 submits that the facts of the said case and the facts of the instant case being almost similar the defendant appellant is entitled to get, the benefit of the said decision and, as such, he being a statutory tenant under section 2 (8) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance 1963 which is similar to section 2 (Umma) of the Premises Rent Control Act 1991, he is entitled to get protection of the Act. Thus he submits that since, after the expiry of the agreement on 31-12-1996 the tenant had been paying rent with the Rent Controller within 15th day of the month following, as provided under section 18 (5) of the Act, 1991, the defendant appellant is not a defaulter as such is not liable to be evicted on such ground. He next submits that the learned Judge of the trial Court was wrong in calculating the rent for the scheduled premises, to be paid by the defendant appellant (tenant) after the expiry of the agreements, by deducting Taka 53200 (the rent deposited with the Rent Controller) from Taka 60,000 the compensation money @ of Taka 2000 per day, inspite of the fact that the same is admittedly the compensation money for' each day's possession. Thus the direction to pay Taka 7,44,000 upon deducting from the total amount of rent paid to the House Rent Controller and also upon deducting the security money, kept with the landlords is also illegal and liable to be set aside. He submits that the compensation can never be regarded as rent and if the defendant appellant is liable to pay the compensation then the plaintiff can recover the same in accordance with law, if necessary, by filing a separate suit But under no circumstances the compensation can be considered as rent and, as such, the direction in that regard is illegal and liable to be set aside. Lastly, Mr Alam frankly admits that till 31- 12-1996 the agreements were in force and the ten- ant, according to the terms of the said agreement, was liable to pay rent within the "first week" of every month, but it appears, that the rent for the month of December 1996, the last month of the tenant period, was not paid within time as per agreement rather the payment was made out of time by only one day. According to him since the defendant never defaulted in paying rent during the tenancy period and subsequently. as he is depositing the same with the House Rent Controller regularly according to law, the conduct of the defendant appellant is very clear and. as such, he should not be evicted from the suit premises on the ground of default. Rather, relying 011 the decision of Kalu Mondal vs Begum Fazilatun Nessa, reported in 46 DLR (AD) 53 he submits that the defendant's clear conduct should be taken into consideration and the delay of only one day in paying rent only for the last month of the tenancy period should be considered leniently and on enquiry, as contemplated in section 18 as to whether the tenant was entitled to the benefit of protection from ejectment at the instance of the landlord due to non-payment of rent, becomes all the more necessary when the tenant comes with a positive case, supported by evidence, that due to some kind of abnormal situation supervening at the relevant time it was beyond his control to pay rent and, as such, the tenant be allowed to remain in the suit premises. 

 12. Heard the learned Advocates of both the parties and perused the record. From the facts and circumstances stated hereinabove and the submissions of the learned Advocates it appears that admittedly the appellant, since his predecessor's time was a tenant under the predecessor of the respondent. Subsequently, the tenancy agreements were executed afresh between them on 22-1-1995 under agreement that the tenancy period would expire on 31-12-1996 and under no circumstances the period would be extended any further. It was also agreed that the tenant will vacate the premises immediately after 31-12-1996. In case the tenant fails to vacate the same he shall pay Taka 2,000 to the landlord, as compensation for each days of overstay till vacating. Further the parties agreed to pay rent of Taka 52,000 within the first week of every month. Under such circumstances we find that the matter in controversy in this suit/appeal is very simple i.e. whether the defendant appellant, being a tenant under the plaintiff respondents, is a defaulter by any means at any time during the subsistence of the tenancy agreement or subsequent thereto and whether he is entitled to got protection under section 18(5) of the Premises Rent Control Act and whether he violated the terms of the agreements and, as such, liable to be evicted? However to answer the question raised section 18( I) and 18(5) of the Premises Rent Control Act are required to be looked into in this respect. 

 13. Upon reading the aforesaid provisions of law it is clear that the provisions are equally safe- guarding the interest of both landlord and the tenant meaning the landlord cannot evict the tenant if the tenant performs his part of duties as incorporated in the agreement including paying the entire rent within the time as specified in the agreement and comply with the other terms of the same as specified therein. In the instant case since a specific date has been fixed, mutually, by the parties in the following manner : “প্রতি মাসে অগ্রিম ভাড়া চলতি মাসের প্রথম সপ্তাহের মধ্যে দ্বিতীয় পক্ষ প্রথম পক্ষকে প্রদান করবেন।” the tenant is to pay the rent accordingly and the time fixed in the law (section 18(5) (Ka)) does not require to be called into and in case the tenant fails to pay accordingly, he becomes a defaulter. It is the specific case of the plaintiff landlords that the defendant tenant did not pay rent for the month of December within time which from the written statement as well as from the cross examination, appears to have been admitted. In his cross examination, the defendant tenant, as DW 1, admitted that ‘১৯৯৬ ইং সালের ডিসেম্বর মাসের ৮ তারিখের মধ্যে দেই।’ So from his own admission it is found that the tenant admitted that although the time specified in the agreement for payment of rent was first week of that month but he did not pay rent for the month of December within that time. The tenant whose default has been established by his own admission, he is not entitled to get any statutory protection against eviction. This view finds support in the case of Binning and Co vs Nasirabad Properties Ltd (40 DLR (AD) 89). The duty is always upon the tenant to take care that he does not become a defaulter. Thus the finding of the trial Court as to payment of rent for the month of Deember'96 is beyond the stipulated period of the agreements for which the tenant cannot avoid the mischief of law and since he is admittedly a defaulter in paying rent, at least for one month during the tenancy period he, under the statute, is nor entitled to get protection of law as provided under section 18(5)(ka) of the Premises Rent Control Act 1991' is found to be in accordance with law. 

 22. So, from the above it appears that the tenant appellant admitted that he constructed the tin-shed structures in the vacant space of the suit premises without prior permission or consent of the plaintiff landlords and, as such, he admitted that he. violated the terms of agreements and thus acted contrary to section 108(p) of the Transfer of Property Act which makes him liable to come within the mischief of section 18(1)(Ka) of the Premises Rent Control Act, and binds himself to vacate the suit premises for which he is not entitled to get any protection of law from eviction even if he is not found to be a defaulter in payment of rent. Under such circumstances the tenant cannot avoid eviction under section 18(1)(ka) of the Act 1991 for violating the terms of the agreement. 

 23. Considering the facts and circumstances stated hereinabove and the decisions referred to by the parties and also on the basis of the principle laid down in the case of Md Nasiruddin vs Md Mizanur Rahman, Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1300 of 2006 (BSCD 2008 page 121) "Even the tenant cannot resist h is eviction if he is found defaulter for one month only and the Premises rent Control Act requires that the tenant must pay the monthly rent in terms of section 18 within the prescribed period to get protection from eviction and not other- wise," we are of the view that the defendant appellant tenant has been proved to be a "defaulter" on his own admission, for nonpayment of rent for the month of December 1996 and also guilty of "violating the terms of the lease agreements" admittedly by constructing structures on the vacant apace of the vacant space of the suit premises and, as such, is not entitled to get any protection from eviction under section 18(1) and 18(5) of the Act. In this respect we find substance in the submissions of Mr Rahman. Thus the defendant appellant tenant is liable to be evicted. Accordingly, the findings of the trial court, complained of herein in this appeal, is hereby affirmed. But so far the calculation to pay Taka 7,44,000 by the trial court, we are of the view that since compensation or security cannot be adjusted with the rent, hence the aforesaid direction of payment is wrong and, as such, the same is liable to be set aside. 

 24. For the reasons and discussions made hereinabove the appeal is allowed in part. The defendant tenant is a defaulter and guilty of violating the terms of the agreement as such liable to be evicted from the suit premises. The defendant appellant tenant is accordingly directed to vacate the suit premises within 30 days, upon removing the unauthorized structures situated on the suit premises in default the plaintiff respondent will be at liberty to get the decree executed in accordance with law. But the finding calculation and direction of the Trial Court to pay Taka 7,44,000 to the landlords being not in accordance with law the same is set aside. However, the plaintiff respondent landlords are entitled to withdraw/receive the rents deposited with the House Rent Controller since January 1997 till vacating the suit premises in accordance with law.
justice_names: Mr. Justice Md. Abu Zafor Siddique

parties:
Kazi Shamsul Huq & others ------ Appellants
VS.
Rabeya Begum & others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
2. Short facts are that the predecessors of the plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No.73 of 1976 in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Comilla for declaration of title and for recovery of khas possession. The suit was decreed on contest on 30.09.1980 and Title Execution Case No.18 of 1980 was filed for execution of the decree after evicting the trespasser defendants therefrom. The judgment-debtor then filed 1st Appeal No.20 of 1981 before the High Court Division and by the judgment and decree dated 07.07.1996 the trial court's decree was modified. The judgment-debtor filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 689 of 1996 before the Appellate Division and obtained an order of stay. The Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 689 of 1996 was dismissed on 16.03.1997 where upon the judgment-debtor filed Civil Review Petition No.14 of 1997 but the same was dis-missed for default no 16.11.2000. The decree-holder, however, filed Title Execution Case No. 3 of 2002 on 08.06.2006 through bonafide mistake forgetting about the tendency of the earlier Title Execution Case No.18 of 1980 and subsequently filed an application for withdrawal of the subsequent Execution Case which was rejected on 03.09.2002. The decree holder thereupon prayed for amendment of the execution petition and also praying for deputing a Magistrate with police force along with an Advocate Commissioner to deliver possession. But the learned joint District Judge by order dated 03.09.2002 allowed the amendment petition and vacated the order of stay and passed necessary orders for proceeding with the Title Execution Case No.18 of 1980. The Judgment-debtors, however, filed an application stating that in the meantime, the Title Execution Case No. 18 of 1980 became barred by limitation under the provision of Article 182 of the Limitation Act and learned Joint District Judge after hearing the parties rejected the said application by order dated 28.09.2002 and directed issuance of the writ of delivery of possession in the instant case. The Judgment-debtors thereafter filed Civil Revision Case No.5090 of 2002 impugning the said order with the averment that the decree-holders filed the Execution Case No. 18 of 1980 in time but when the decree was modified by the Court of appeal below in First Appeal No. 02 of 1981 by the judgment and decree dated 07.07.1996 drawn on 03.11.1996, the decree-holders ought to have taken steps in the Execution Case in aid of the execution of the same as per modification within 3 years from the date of at least within 3 years from the date of dismissal of the Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal and accordingly the execution case is barred by limitation as no step has been taken within 3 years from the dismissal of the leave petition. The High Court Division made the Rule absolute setting aside the orders dated 03.09.2002 and 28.09.2002 allowing to proceed with the Execution Case No. 18 of 1980. 

 5. It is not disputed that the Title Suit No. 73 of 1976 brought by predecessors of plaintiffs in the First Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Comilla for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession was decreed on contest on 30.09.1980 and Title Execution case No: 18 of 1980 was started for taking delivery of possession in the suit land. It is on record the judgment-debtor filed First Appeal No.20 of 1981 before the High Court Division and the decree of the trial court was modified by the High Court Division by judgment dated 07.07.1996. The judgment debtor then filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 689 of 1996 before the Appellate Division and obtained an order of stay. The said Civil Petition for leave to Appeal No. 689 of 1996 was dismissed on 16.03.1997. The Judgment debtor then filed Civil Review Petition No. 14 of 1997, which was dismissed for default on 16.11.2000. Thereafter, the decree holder filed Title Execution Case No. 3 of 2002 on 08.06.2002 through bonafide mistake forgetting about the pendency of the earlier Title Execution Case No.18 of 1980 and later on filed an application for withdrawal of the subsequent title execution case which was rejected on 03.09.2002. But the learned Joint District Judge by order dated 03.09.2002 allowed the Title Execution Case No. 18 of 1980 to proceed. Thereafter, judgment debtor filed an application, stating that the Title Execution Case No. 18 of 1980 has in the meantime become barred by limitation under the Provision of Article 182 of the Limitation Act and the learned Joint District Judge upon hearing the parties rejected the said application by order dated 28.09.2002. The Judgment debtors then filed Civil Revision No. 5090 of 2002 impugning the said order and the Rule was made absolute by the High Court Division by the impugned judgment. 

 6. Mr. Bhuiyan submits that the learned single Judge of the High Court Division erred in law in holding that Article 182 (5) of the Limitation Act applies in the instant case and the Title Execution Case No. 18 of 1980 is barred, by limitation as no step in aid was taken within 3(three) years inasmuch as the said Article of the Limitation Act has got no manner of application in the present case when the Title Execution Case No. 18 of 1980 was pending before the said execution Court. He further submits that the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division erred in law in applying Article 182 (5) of the Limitation Act, overlooking the provisions laid down in Article 182(3) of the Limitation Act providing for 3(three) years-time after the passing of the final order in review application. He next submits that the decree holder appellants were not required to file an application for proceeding with the pending Title of 1980 as it was the duty of the executing court to proceed with the same suo-motu and the said Title Execution Case being a pending one was not barred by limitation in view of the principles of law enunciated by the Appellate Division in the case of Shah Newaz Ebne Mostaque and others Vs. Shah Alam and others reported in 55 DLR (AD) 69. 

 8. In 55 DLR (AD) 69 case although the facts are a bit different, it was held that the decree-holder was not required to file an application for proceeding with the pending execution case as it was the duty of the Court to proceed with the same suo-moto. In the case of Baburam Lal and another Vs. Debdas Lala reported in AIR 1959 Calcutta 73, it was held that while it is settled law that the decree of the appellate Court supersedes the original decree passed by the trial court, it does no necessarily follow that the execution proceedings already instituted became dead. It was reasonable to consider that on and from the passing of a decree by the Court of appeal, the application which was originally for execution of the trial Court's decree becomes an application for the execution of the appellate Court's decree. Where in an appeal the decree is modified in such a manner that the proceedings can still of on, it will be for the Court concerned to decide whether it will allow necessary amendment of the application for execution in order that it may become property an application for execution of the appellate Court's decree. In the case of Chauthilal Vs. Badri Prasad and another reported in AIR 1960 Rajasthan 249, it was held that as under: "The authorities, which lay down that the decree of the trial court gets merged in the decree of the appellate court are no doubt correct, but the said decisions only emphasise this fact when dealing with the question of limitation as to when the period of limitation will commence for execution of the decree, or when the point in dispute is as to what court can amend the decree. 

 The learned counsel for the respondent had placed before us the case of L. Bengali Mal and others Vs. Baijnath prasad and others reported in AIR 1942 Allahabad 338 and submitted that in that case it was held that the words "where there has been a review of judgment" in Article 182(3) must be interpreted strictly as meaning what they say. Article 182(3) applies only where review application has been allowed and there has been actual review or re-hearing. Article 182(3) has no application where review application is rejected. In the instant case, the original Title Execution case no.18 of 1980 was pending and the subsequent Execution case No.3 of 2002 filed by the decree holder though inadvertence during pendency of the earlier Titles Execution Case No.18 of 1980 was subsequently rejected and the decree holder was allowed to proceed with the pending Execution case No.18 of 1980.

parties:
Harendra Nath Mahali ------ Appellant
Vs.
Ramesh Chandra Halder and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
2. The Miscellaneous case was filed stating, inter alia, that the pre-emptor is a co sharer of the holding land of which 'has been transferred by the kabala dated May 26, 1980 by the opposite party No.2, a co-sharer of the holding (in the Miscellaneous case) to the opposite party No. 1, (in the Miscellaneous case), a stranger without serving any notice under section 89 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, that he came to know about the transfer on Falgoon, 1387 BS and that on obtaining certified copy on February 27, 1981 had the definite knowledge about the transfer by the opposite party No.2 (in the Miscellaneous petition), that as the opposite party No.1, the transferee (preemptee) is a stranger purchaser in the holding of which he is a co sharer and, as such, as per provision of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act he is entitled to pre-empt the transfer made by the kabala dated 26-5-1980. 

 4. The trial Court dismissed the Miscellaneous case on the findings that the same is not barred by limitation and. that also not bad for defect of party but the pre-emptor is not entitled to preempt the transfer that took place on 26-5-1980 since the purchaser (preemptee) as per agreement for reconveyance has already reconveyed the land to his vendor (opposite party No. 2 in the Miscellaneous case) on 1-3-1983. 

 10. The undenied position is, that while the Miscellaneouscase case filed under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was pending the land sought to be preempted was reconveyed by the transferee to the original vendor. It was the case of the opposite party Nos.1 and 2 (buyer and seller) that on the date of transfer sought to be preempted an 'Ekrarnama' was given by the transferee that on repayment of the money he would return the land to the seller. In the background of the stipulation in the 'Ekrarnama' or agreement for reconveyance, the buyer (preemptee) reconveyed the land to the original vendor. The trial Court rejected the prayer for preemption since the subject matter of preemption had gone back to the original owner. The appellate Court reversed the said finding on the observation as mentioned hereinbefore. The High Court Division restored the judgment of the trial Court on the finding that on the very date of transfer an agreement for reconveyance was executed by the transferee (preemptee) and that in terms of agreement for reconveyance the purchaser has re- conveyed the land to the seller (original owner) and he is in possession. It may be mentioned the High Court Division as well as the trial Court on due consideration of the evidence held that after reconveyance the original owner is in possession of the land. Since the appellate Court did not discuss the evidence as was required by the law while reversing the judgment of the trial Court the High Court Division scrutinised the evidence and thereupon arrived at the finding that the evidence is sufficient on the record showing the genuineness of the assertion of the original owner that on the date of sale the buyer executed an agreement for reconveyance and that in terms of agreement for re conveyance the buyer reconveyed the land and the original owner is in possession. The fact of execution of the agreement of reconveyance was proved by the OPW No.3, the scribe of the sale deed. 

 11. The law is settled now that prior to the filing of the petition seeking preemption if the land goes back to the original owner the right of preemption does no longer exist but if the reconveyance is a collusive one i.e. if the right, title and interest do not pass to the original owner and  that possession remains with the buyer i.e. pre- emptee in that case even if there is reconveyance of the land prior to the filing of the petition seeking preemption the right of preemption would not be lost. The law is also settled now that if a transfer is burdened with the agreement for reconveyance the right of preemption would not be defeated but the preemptor would take the land so preempted with the encumbrance of reconveyance. This view was held in the case of Biswaswar Roy vs Joytennessa and others reported in 13 DLR 287. The view expressed in the aforesaid case has been found to be correct by the Appellate Division in the case of Shafi Khan vs Mannujan Hussain and others reported in 35 DLR (AD) 225 wherein it has been observed "when a transfer is made on condition for reconveyance, the right of preemption is subject to this condition for reconveyance is found to be correct being in accord with section 40 of the Transfer of Property Act as well as with reason". 

 12. In the case reported in 35 DLR (AD) 225 it has been held "The main question for careful examination will be whether he actually got back his land, and if the answer is in the affirmative, the position will be as if no transfer was at all made by him. If, however, it is found that the resale is a colourable show up or a mere paper transaction and that right, title and interest in the land have not gone back to the vendor but still remain vested in the transferee then the re-sale may be ignored and preemption may be allowed". 

 13. In the case of Muzaffar Ali Bepari vs Omar Ali and others reported in 1 BLC (AD) 25 it has been held that in case a reconveyance is for the purpose of defeating the right of preemption and that the reconveyance is a collusive one through the clandestine understanding between the buyer (preemptee) and the seller (original owner) and that the transfer is a colourable and sham transaction and that the pre-emptee, in fact, did not part with the possession of the land allegedly shown to have been reconveyed to the original owner, a reconveyance of the aforesaid nature would not affect the right of preemption. 

 14. From the trend of reported decisions it is seen that even if during pendency of the case seeking preemption if in the background of an agreement for reconveyance, genuineness whereof has been established by reliable evidence, the right of preemption is not available. The matters which are to be looked into in a situation where right of preemption is not available because of the reconveyance either prior to the filing of the petition seeking preemption or during the pendency of the case seeking preemption as to whether the reconveyance so made is a colourable and sham transaction and whether the right, title and interest because of the reconveyance have gone back to the original owner and whether the preemptee has parted with the possession of the land. If the reconveyance is tainted with one of the aforesaid factors, then right of preemption would not be affected. Once genuineness of the agreement for reconveyance is established by the original owner and that because of the agreement for reconveyance the buyer (preemptee) had reconveyed the land and the right, title and interest have passed to the original owner and that the land so reconveyed is possessed by the original owner, in that situation the prayer for preemption would not be allowed or, in other words, preemption would not be granted. 

 15. In the instant case from the materials on record it is seen that genuineness of the agreement for reconveyance has been established by reliable evidence and it has also been established that after the reconveyance right, title and interest in the land sought to be preempted have gone back to the original owner and that he is in possession of the land so reconveyed. There is nothing on record to show that the reconveyance in the instant case was a colourable and sham transaction or, in other words, was not a genuine one or the reconveyance has been made with the object of defeating the right of preemption. 

 17. It is seen that the original owner is actually prosecuting the case after reconveyance at all stages.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.670 of 2004
parties:
Md. Mizanur Rahman ----- Petitioner
Versus
Tahera Begum and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Mr. Syed .J. R. Mudassir Husain, C.J:- This civil petition for leave to appeal, at the instance of plaintiff, is directed against the judgment and order dated 16-03-2004 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.5242 of 2002 making the Rule absolute upon setting aside the order dated 27-07-2002 passed by the Joint District Judge in Title Suit No. 12 of 2002 staying all further proceedings of Title Execution Case No.01 of 2002. 

 2. The facts leading to this petition, are that one Md. Mohsin Khan, predecessor-in-interest of the defendant-respondent Nos.I-5 as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No.22 of 1994 on 27-04-1994 for partition; upon hearing the parties the said partition suit was decreed on 09-05-1996 against the defendant-respondent Nos. 143, 144 and 232 and ex-parte against the rest in preliminary form and after receipt of the report of the Advocate Commissioner effecting partition the said preliminary decree was made final on 25-07-2001 and thereupon the said plaintiff-respondents put the final decree in execution by filing Title Execution Case No.01 of 2002 for possession of the suit property. 

 3. In the meantime. the leave-petitioner as plaintiff filed Title Suit No.I2 of 2002 on 16-06-2002 for setting aside the aforesaid final decree dated 25-07-2001 passed in the aforesaid Title Suit No,22 of 1994 along with order dated 04-06-2002 for requisition of the police force for giving delivery of possession of the property passed in the said Title Execution Case No.01 of 2002. His main case was that by two deeds dated 07-01-1997 and 03-03 I 997 he along with his two brothers purchased the entire share of Jalal Patwary the defendant-respondent No.234 and the same was allotted to him in the preliminary decree dated 09-05-1996. It has been further stated that the said Jalal Patwary died on 28-05-2000, but the preliminary decree was made final against him without bringing his legal representatives on record and as such the final decree being nullity the aforesaid execution case was liable to be dismissed. 

 4. On 27-06-2002, the plaintiff-petitioner made an application under Section 15I read with Order 21 Rule 26 of the Code of Civil Procedure in his suit for stay of all further proceedings of the said Title Execution Case No.1 of 2002 mainly on the ground that final decree was drawn against dead person named, Jalal Patwary defendant-respondent No.234 being a nullity can not be executed. 

 5. Md. Mohsin Khan, predecessor-in-interest of the defendant-respondents opposed the aforesaid application dated 27-06-2002 by filing counter affidavit and denied the material allegations made in the application. Upon hearing the parties the learned Joint District Judge stayed all further proceedings of Title Execution Case No.01 of 2002 by his order dated 27-06-2002 and challenging the aforesaid order, the respondents moved the High Court Division in revision and the learned Judges of the High Court Division made the Rule absolute. Hence, this leave-petition by the petitioner as plaintiff of Title Suit No. 12 of 2002. 

 6. Mr. Mahbubey Alam, the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioner, contended that Jalal Patwary admittedly died during process of final decree which was within full knowledge of Md. Mohshin Khan, the plaintiff of the original Title Suit No.22 of 1994 having also knowledge of deposition of predecessor in interest of the deceased Jalal Patwary upon the petitioner No.1 and his two brothers with malafide intention did neither substitute the heirs of the deceased Jalal Patwary nor impleaded the petitioner and his two brothers in order to obtain fraudulent final decree and as such the High Court Division having totally misconceived erred in law in holding the view that the application of the petitioner No. 1 for stay made under Order 21 Rule 26 read with Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure in Title Suit No, 12 of 2002 as not maintainable. Learned Counsel further contended that the High Court Division committed an error of law holding that the learned Joint District Judge acted in excess of jurisdiction in granting stay of all further proceedings of Title Execution Case No. 1 of 2002 by filing the aforesaid Title Suit No. 12 of 2002. 

 7. Mr. Joynal Abedin, the learned Counsel appearing for the respondents, supporting the impugned judgment of the High Court Division, contended that the High Court Division having considered the facts and circumstances of the case rightly found that the application of the petitioner for stay made under Order 21 Rule 26 of the Code of Civil Procedure in Title Suit No. 12 of 2002 is wholly misconceived and that under Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure is equally not maintainable and the learned Joint District Judge acted in excess of his jurisdiction in granting stay in Title Suit No.12 of 2002 of all Further proceedings of Title Execution Case No, 1 of 2002 filed by the respondents. 

 Meanwhile, said Mohsin Khan took steps for partition and the Advocate Commissioner appointed submitted his report effecting partition of the suit land. The Court accepted the report in due course and mad eth preliminary decree final on 25-07-2001. Said Mohsin then put the decree into execution in aforesaid Title Execution Case No.1 of 2002 for possession of his share. Opposite party No.1 however preferred not to take any step either for his substitution or addition in place of said decreed Jalal Patwary in the suit. He also did not raise any objection to the execution of the decree before the executing Court. 

 Instead, as stated above opposite party No. 1 instituted Title Suit No, 12 of 2002 against the petitioners and others for setting aside the final decree and all orders passed in the execution case. 

 "What surprised us most is if opposite parity No.1 was so sure that their predecessor-in-interest defendant No.232 Jalal Patwary died on 28-05-2000 then why he did no take any step thereto in Title Suit No.22 of 1994 and why he allowed the preliminary decree to be made final against said deceased Jalal Patwary. In 1997, he purchased the entire share of said Jalal Patwary that was allotted to him in the preliminary decree. So, he could not claim that he was not aware of said decree. In the fitness of things, most natural and proper step for said opposite party No.1 was to take step for substitution or addition in place of deceased defendant No.232 Jalal Patwary in the suit. 

 Instead, on 16-06-2002 opposite party No. 1 instituted Title Suit No. 12 of 2002 for setting aside the final decree on the ground of nullity. Even in 2002 opposite party No, 1 could have achieved very same objective by taking step before the executing Court which is the only forum to decide whether the decree was still valid for execution; But he has not taken any step before the executing Court challenging the final decree till date".

parties:
Ful Meher Bibi being dead her heirs Sabura Khatun and others ------ Appellants
Vs.
Abdul Wahab and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
2. Short facts are that the plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 285 of 1980 for partition in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Dhaka, impleading Ful Meher  Bibi and thirteen others as the defendants. The suit was subsequently renumbered as Partition Suit No. 113 of 1991 on transfer. The suit land originally belonged to Sheikh Nazimuddin and Abdus Salam, sons of late Raizuddin in equal shares. Sheikh Nazimuddin died leaving behind one son, Abdur Rahman and one daughter, Amirjan. Plaintiffs are the heirs and successors of Abdus Salam who inherited to the extent of the other half of the suit land. The suit was ultimately decreed in preliminary and final form on 25.08.1992 and 05.07.1993 respectively, though the appellants claim that no summons of the original suit was served upon Ful Meher Bibi (defendant No.8). The case of the appellants is that Ful Meher Bibi was married more than forty years back and since then she had been residing at her husband's house. But the plaintiff respondents fraudulently obtained the ex-parte decree in question showing service of summons upon her by hanging at her paternal house instead of serving it at her husband's house where she was residing in order to deprive her from contesting the suit. The appellants further claim that the plaintiffs were fully aware of her correct address of Ful Meher Bibi as they are her co-sharers. The appellants came to know about the ex-parte decree when the process server went to the suit land for execution of the ex-parte decree passed in the above mentioned partition suit. The appellants then filed Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 1994 under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the preliminary and final decrees in question and for restoration of the original suit to its original file and number. 

 4. The learned Subordinate Judge (now joint District Judge), Dhaka, allowed the miscellaneous case on the ground that summons of the original suit was not duly served upon Ful Meher Bibi and restored the suit to its original file and number. The respondent then filed Civil Revision No.2951 of 1998 before the High Court Division and the Rule issue was made absolute. The High Court Division while making the Rule absolute observed that the application under order 9 rule 13 was barred by limitation and no application for condonation of delay was filed. It was further observed that the preliminary decree of the original suit was passed on 25.08.1992 and the final decree was passed on 05.07.1993 but the application under order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure was filed on 09.03.1994. The High Court Division further noticed that one Md. Ramjan Ali had sworn affidavit as the nephew (sister's son) of Ful Meher Bibi but he did not turn up to depose in support of the application rather one Raham Ali claiming to be a nephew (brother's son) of Ful Meher Bibi deposed in the case under order 9 rule 13 of Code of Civil Procedure. It was further observed that after the death of Ful Meher Bibi, as claimed by Raham Ali, none of her children came before the court to support the application nor authorized Raham Ali to depose on their behalf. The High Court Division further observed that service by hanging is not uncommon in the country side. 

 7. It is undisputed that Ful Meher Bibi was defendant No. 8 in original Title Suit No.285 of 1980 subsequently renumbered as Partition Suit No.113 of 1991. In the plaint of the partition suit it was stated that the suit property belonged to Sheikh Nazimuddin who died leaving behind one son, Abdur Rahman and one daughter, Amirjan as his legal heirs and successors. Defendant No.8, Ful Meher Bibi was one of daughters of Amirjan, daughter of Sheikh Nazimuddin. 

 8. It is on record that Ful Meher Bibi was one of the principal defendants in the suit. It is also undisputed that she was married about 40-45 years ago with one Sharbat Ali of the same village Kamrangirchar but in the plaint she was made a party as daughter of Moksed Ali along with her other sisters and brother showing her address at her paternal house. It is also undisputed that summons of the original suit was served on her by hanging on the outer door of the dwelling but of her paternal home. 

 10. The trial court held that it was incumbent upon the plaintiffs of the original suit to make defendant No. 8 a party showing address at her husband's house and summons of the suit ought to have been sent to that address but that was not done. 

 12. Order V Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that, "Where the defendant or his agent or such other person as aforesaid refuses to sign the acknowledgement, or where the serving officer, after using all due and reasonable diligence, cannot find the defendant, and there is no agent empowered to accept service of the summons on his behalf, nor any other person on whom service can be made, the serving officer shall affix a copy of the summons on the outer door or some other conspicuous part of the house in which the defendant ordinarily resides or carries on business or personally works for gain, and shall then return the original to the Court from which it was issued, with a report endorsed thereon or annexed thereto stating that he has so affixed the copy, the circumstances under which he did so, and the name and address of the person (if any) by whom the house was identified and in whose presence the copy was affixed." 

 13. In the instant case, undisputedly summons of the original suit upon defendant No.8, Ful Meher Bibi (since deceased) was not served by hanging on her dwelling but where she ordinarily resided nor summons was sent to that address rather the same was issued and alleged to have been served by hanging on the outer door of dwelling but of her paternal house where she did not reside for the last 40-45 years. The case of the appellant-petitioners in the case under Order IX Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure was that defendant No. 8 for the first time came to know of the ex parte decree on 09.02.1994 when the process server of the Court went to the locality to deliver possession of land in execution of the decree in question and thereafter she filed the case and from the date of her knowledge she was within time. 

 15. From our above discussions, we are of the view that the findings of the trial court are based on the materials on record that there was no service of summons upon Ful Meher Bibi, defendant No. 8 of the original suit. Therefore, it was no function of the High Court Division to sit in appeal over that finding of the trial court in revisional jurisdiction. We also find that the application order 9 rules 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not barred by limitation in the facts of this case as limitation is to be counted from the date of knowledge of defendant No. 8 under Article 164 of the Limitation Act as the summons was not duly served upon her.
